speechtext:

The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) is reported to have said recently that if South Africa refuses independence for Namibia, Canada would consider supporting international sanctions against that country. As the United Nations has clearly declared the independence of Namibia and indeed has passed resolutions
calling for sanctions against that country, and since this involves respect for the rule of law and the right of the majority to choose their government, I move, seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt):

ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM POSSIBILITY OF MANITOBA RENEWING AGREEMENT-CONTINGENCY PLAN IF PROVINCES WITHDRAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a question being raised at the federal-provincial conference of ministers of finance concerns the future of the AIB program, and, as the Prime Minister knows, it was reported that the province of Manitoba may not renew its anti-inflation program agreement when its first term expires this March, while other provinces are reviewing their commitment to the program, will

the Prime Minister tell the House first if Manitoba has informed his government that it will not renew its agreement, as reported and, secondly, whether his administration will continue with the anti-inflation program if one or more provinces decide to let their agreement expire?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM POSSIBILITY OF MANITOBA RENEWING AGREEMENT-CONTINGENCY PLAN IF PROVINCES WITHDRAW
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am informed by the parliamentary secretary that that item has not been reached yet and, therefore, discussion has not begun on it. My knowledge of the Manitoba situation goes back a month or two when Manitoba indicated that it might want to seek some changes in the regulation or in the application of the controls rather than suggest it would withdraw from the program completely.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM POSSIBILITY OF MANITOBA RENEWING AGREEMENT-CONTINGENCY PLAN IF PROVINCES WITHDRAW
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the Prime Minister inform the House of the nature of any federal contingency plans that may be put in place to keep the program going in the event one or more provinces decides not to extend the agreement?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM POSSIBILITY OF MANITOBA RENEWING AGREEMENT-CONTINGENCY PLAN IF PROVINCES WITHDRAW
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, you will realize that the question is hypothetical in its form. I intend discussing this matter at the first ministers' conference in a general way. Of course, it may be necessary to have federal-provincial meetings in the new year to discuss the eventualities the hon. member suggests. For the time being we are taking it as the fact that the provinces will want to co-operate with the federal government in its anti-inflation program as long as the program is in place.

subtopic: PLANS FOR RESTRAINING WAGE INCREASES FOLLOWING THE LIFTING OF CONTROLS
PLANS FOR RESTRAINING WAGE INCREASES FOLLOWING THE LIFTING OF CONTROLS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the finance ministers continue to negotiate they are obviously concerned with what happens on the termination of controls, whenever that happens. On Tuesday last the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board, Mr. Pepin, told the Standing Committee on Finance that there is a great danger of an explosion in wage rates at the end of controls because AIB wage rulings do not affect the composition of contracts, but only roll back for a temporary period any wage increases in excess of its guidelines. Will the Prime Minister tell the House whether such an eventuality was contemplated when the program was planned, bearing in mind that, if Mr. Pepin's statement is correct, we will require new legislation to ensure that such a bounce back does not occur?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: PLANS FOR RESTRAINING WAGE INCREASES FOLLOWING THE LIFTING OF CONTROLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course that possibility was contemplated and it is part of every argument against controls. It is one of the reasons the federal government, when it finally decided to introduce controls, made the legislation for a sufficient period of time that this kind of difficulty would be discussed during the control period and, hopefully, that the various opinion and decision makers in the economy would themselves want to do away with this kind of eventuality. It must be realized of course that unless the various sectors are prepared to take some position which would guarantee that there is no renewal of inflation
December 6, 1976

after the controls have been lifted that would make it very difficult to shorten the time of the control period.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ON DISADVANTAGED PROVINCES-PROPOSALS FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary in respect of the meeting of finance ministers. Last June I questioned the Prime Minister about the possible negative effect of the proposed fiscal arrangement amendments on the have-not provinces. He assured this House then that the changes would prove advantageous to those provinces. In view of statements to the contrary by a number of provincial ministers can the Prime Minister now state definitely that these proposals will maintain the previous commitment to narrow the disparity in social services between provinces and in particular take into account the increasing phenomenon of very high unemployment in these particular provinces.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ON DISADVANTAGED PROVINCES-PROPOSALS FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, on the last part of the question the proposals are not by themselves directly meant to deal with the unemployment problem. They have to do with social services, post-secondary education and medical and hospital care being part of the social services. The fact that some provinces object to them is not surprising. The provinces all come to Ottawa in the hope of getting a greater transfer of money or tax points. This is part of the routine of federal-provincial conferences. I told the House last year and I repeat now that these programs as they are being proposed, particularly the establishment of interim financing proposals, are meant to give the provinces a much greater degree of autonomy in the application of their programs and will still guarantee they will get the money necessary to fulfill those programs.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ON DISADVANTAGED PROVINCES-PROPOSALS FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister would recognize as well as all hon. members the relationship between the three issues being discussed in the health-welfare, educational and social service area, but with the growing problem of unemployment and the fears which have been expressed about a resulting uneven development of social services across Canada or as one of the provincial ministers referred to it, the balkanization, what guarantees is the federal government offering which would assist the provinces with a narrow tax base to make the same per capita provincial contribution to social services as their richer counterparts?

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ON DISADVANTAGED PROVINCES-PROPOSALS FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, the way the programs are established, the proposal made is that part of the transfer will be in cash and that cash paid will be the same to every province regardless of whether it is wealthy or poor. The advantage of this of course is that under the previous type of scheme the wealthier provinces could afford to spend more of
Oral Questions
the 50 cent dollars because they could put up their own 50 per cent of the spending required. This particular portion of the program is meant to be more equitable to the less wealthy provinces because it will not be demanded of them that they spend any percentage. We will just give them that portion of the grant regardless of the amount they spend and it will not be tied with their capacity to spend or to their financial base.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ON DISADVANTAGED PROVINCES-PROPOSALS FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the position earlier enunciated by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, I wonder whether the Prime Minister could confirm whether or not the have-not provinces are in agreement with this or have registered their belief that the quality of their own services will in effect either remain static or deteriorate, thus widening the gap between the poorer provinces and those that are more wealthy.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ON DISADVANTAGED PROVINCES-PROPOSALS FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is asking me to confirm the position of the provinces. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance just informed me that the provinces have not expressed their views on that yet this morning. take effect over the successive economic periods and they will have the effect of stimulating the economy and employment.

9,000	forestry workers being laid off in British Columbia and an unemployment level exceeding 10 per cent in the province of Quebec-one could list the problems associated with every province in the country-will the Prime Minister reassess the government's position and do now what president elect Carter has announced recently in the United States, that is, set specific targets for the next couple of years by which to measure the economic performance of the government and reduce over the next two years unemployment to acceptable full employment levels, but set targets now to which we can hold the government obligated in terms of its accomplishments?

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-POSSIBILITY OF NEW PROPOSALS TO DEAL WITH PROBLEM AND THE SETTING OF TARGETS
speechtext: You are not listening to the Tories now, are you?

LLOYDMINSTER HEAVY OIL DEPOSITS-PLANS TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT-DATE OF REPORT ON EXPORT POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In testimony before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works on November 23 the Minister outlined the strategy of his department with respect to oil production for the future in Canada. In view of the great importance he placed upon the Lloydminster heavy oil deposits for the success of this strategy, I wonder if the minister would advise the House when he expects the National Energy Board's report on oil export policy to be completed. Can he also advise the House what interim measures are now being taken and what further interim measures are being contemplated to ensure that these important oilfields are not irretreiv-ably shut down before the minister's plans for them can begin?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: LLOYDMINSTER HEAVY OIL DEPOSITS-PLANS TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT-DATE OF REPORT ON EXPORT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the first question, I believe that the National Energy Board will be publishing its report some time in the late winter or early spring, I hope by the month of March.
As to the interim measures being taken, they fall into two different categories. The first category is a decision by the National Energy Board to increase the allowance for export from what has been an average of about 80,000 barrels per day of heavy crude oil to 125,000 barrels for the month of January. That is a very substantial increase without any reduction during that month in allocations for light and medium crude.
As to the longer term, I am very hopeful that the discussions with Mr. Getty-and I have had correspondence-will lead to an understanding between the federal government and the government of Alberta for a new set of ground rules which will encourage the development and upgrading of those heavy oils in the Lloydminster area.

subtopic: LLOYDMINSTER HEAVY OIL DEPOSITS-PLANS TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT-DATE OF REPORT ON EXPORT POLICY
speechtext: Having regard to the discussions the minister is having or will have with the Alberta government, can the minister tell the House what specific proposals the government is going to advance not only for increasing production but also, and more importantly, for establishing in Canada refining capabilities, which are very necessary, so that these vast heavy oil reserves can be used to resolve our long term energy problems?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: LLOYDMINSTER HEAVY OIL DEPOSITS-PLANS TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT-DATE OF REPORT ON EXPORT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Getty has agreed that there should be a task force formed, and that task force is in the process of being put together at the present time. It will be headed by my deputy minister, Mr. MacNabb and, I think, by Mr. Govier of the Alberta government. This task force will draw upon both departments of both governments with a view to examining a set of proposals I put forward to Mr. Getty.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce I should like to put a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the new regulations that took effect on November 29 which put quotas on the import of textiles; in view of the fact that many Canadian importers, especially in the Vancouver area, have been caught with their imports for the Christmas selling season in transit and require certificates of clearance for them; in view of the fact that they are being told as of today that it is going to take from 10 to 14 days to get clearances on any particular application, can the Prime Minister advise this House whether he is prepared to take immediate steps and use his good offices to persuade the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to attend to this matter immediately? The situation is causing extremely serious difficulty not just in the city of Vancouver but in other places in Canada as well. I may point out that these are not goods which would be stopped by the import quotas; these are goods which were ordered before the quotas were imposed and which would properly be allowed through. It is just an administrative problem which is causing a great deal of difficulty.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: BILL C-19-DELETION OF CLAUSE 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following extensive consultations on Bill C-19, the government has agreed to support the deletion in committee of clause 15 of that bill, the clause relating to the Railway Act. Pursuant to those same discussions, the government proposes to move at a later date another bill which would have the same effect as clause 15, and the government would not anticipate any procedural difficulties with that move.
With that understanding, Mr. Speaker, I believe the House would give me leave now to move, seconded by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Guay):
That notwithstanding any Standing Order, no later than 3.45 p.m. on December 17, 1976, Mr. Speaker shall interrupt any debate and shall put forthwith and successively any question or questions necessary for the disposal at all stages of Bill C-19, an act to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable the restraint of government expenditures.
I also understand that there would be unanimous consent to make an order that if the debate on second reading of Bill C-19 concludes today, any division or divisions will be held at 3.00 p.m. after questions tomorrow.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: BILL C-19-DELETION OF CLAUSE 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to bother repeating what I said, except to say this: this is an indication of why from time to time the government ought to listen to the members of this House, instead of assuming that it has in its own reservoir of thought all of the wisdom regarding the problems facing Canada. Many members who spoke during the course of the debate told the government repeatedly about the importance of this section. I must say I would be modest in claiming today, for the opposition in this parliament, after long and arduous debate, a victory respecting Bill C-19.
More than that, Mr. Speaker, I think it is only fair to point out to the government that in the event the government see fit to bring forward a bill-they have not said definitely they will, but I understand this may be their intention-then I say as straightforwardly as I always try to be that to the extent we are permitted to press this issue, we intend to do so. I say that because what was wrong with the provision in Bill C-19 would be equally wrong in any bill in which it might be brought forward in substitution for clause 15.
One other matter, Mr. Speaker. I think it is important in terms of this motion that everybody understand that this is not the first time the provisions in Bill C-19 which the government has now undertaken to withdraw, or some similar provisions, have been brought before this House. In the first session of this parliament the government brought forward Bill C-87 which contained this provision in precisely the same terms. Although
Business of the House
there was never any debate on Bill C-87, there was long consultation involving many members of this House regarding the provisions of that bill as they related to the corresponding clause of this bill which the government has now undertaken will be withdrawn.
We pointed out to the government the position of the opposition, as well as the opposition of a host of people in Canada, in view of the importance in terms of confederation on one hand and the shipping industry on the other, and we urged the government to reconsider its position. We hoped, quite frankly, that during the course of the summer the government would reconsider its position and would bring in a bill that at least did not contain that clause.
1 cannot comprehend the workings of the minds of members of the government unless it is that they are completely out of touch with reality. However, following these negotiations carried out in good faith between the responsible minister and a responsible member of the opposition who has been here for many years and who is known as a member not to play games with the government-and I speak of the hon. member for Edmonton West-the government once again, for some reason unknown to us, brought in Bill C-19 including the same clause.
As a result of all these negotiations, it must be clear to any member of the government with even half an eye what the intention of the opposition is in respect of this bill. The importance of this bill to people in many parts of Canada must also be clear. In spite of all this, what did we see? We were faced with the appearance of Bill C-19. Lest some spokesman for the government attempts to point out that this government is responsive to the needs of Canadians in terms of Bill C-19, let me just say that the opposition has had to kick this government in the head to get it to finally see the reasoning behind the objection. Any government that has to be moved in this way, by a kick in the head, cannot be called responsive in terms of any real meaning.
This is an important day for us in this House to understand the tradition of a second reading debate. It is the right of the opposition, when it sees a great principle at stake, to debate a bill and use all reasonable parliamentary procedures to delay the government so that in a country as broad and diverse as this country there will be an opportunity for that point of view to be brought home with pressure placed on the government.
This particular piece of legislation presents the classic argument against the use of the British system of closure. If this debate were taking place under the British system, it would only have lasted one day and this government, as bullheaded as it is from time to time, would have been able to go forward and enact the measure. The damage would then be done and the only recourse would be that provided at an election. This is an indication that perhaps there should be another recourse, and that is the recourse of this parliament to delay legislation when it is bad.
That right of parliament carries with it a corresponding responsibility not to delay good legislation. It has never been

December 6, 1976
Business of the House
the practice of this opposition to argue interminably in respect of legislation that was in keeping with a principle that ought to be accepted.
The members on this side of the House of Commons have done the people of Canada a service today. They have debated this bill long and hard and have finally brought the government to this position. I hope the government will remember this, and will remember as well that the sins of clause 15, if they are transmitted in the same way, will be dealt with similarly in any subsequent bill that is brought forward. It will be the intention of this party, I hope joined by other opposition parties in this House and members on the government side who represent areas in the province of Quebec, in the mari-times and, to the extent there are any, government members from out west, and those from Ontario, to consider any substitution for Bill C-19 which contains a counterpart to clause 15 as being just as bad as the bill is today.
I hope it has been brought home to the government that any legislation which affects something as fundamental as our confederation, as does this bill, as set forth by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain during his memorable speech, should not be brought forward in a willy-nilly fashion in an attempt to override the wishes of the people of this country.
It is becoming abundantly apparent day after day, as a result of the debate on this legislation and as a result of other things that have happened inside and outside this chamber, that this goverment does not have all the answers, or perhaps that this government has none of the answers. In terms of original thought, this government's well has run dry. Its attitude is respect of Bill C-19 is the best indication possible of how dry is its well of wisdom.

subsubtopic: BILL C-19-DELETION OF CLAUSE 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council was quite correct in his statement that there had been consultations leading to the presentation of the motion now before us, and I am pleased to confirm that we shall give our support to that motion.
The effect of what we are doing is that the debate on second reading of Bill C-19 may not last many more days. It might even end today. At any rate, we have the government's assurance that when the bill gets into the standing committee clause 15 will be deleted. It is then understood that further stages of the debate will not last longer than a week from Friday. In return for getting rid of clause 15-and I think clause 16(4) has to go as well-it is reasonable that this long debate should come to some kind of termination.
However, sir, I do not think I can wax quite as eloquently as did the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton about this being a great parliamentary victory. It is a victory, as clause 15 should not have been in this bill and it is to be taken out. However, Mr. Speaker, neither should clauses 6, 7, 8 and 9 have been in this bill. Those are clauses that have denied to families in Canada in 1976 over $200 million, to which they are entitled, in increases in their family allowances. If these clauses had

been taken out as well as clause 15, then perhaps I might be able to say this was a great victory for parliament. It is a victory, but not quite as outstanding a victory as has been suggested by my friend, the House leader of the official opposition.
There are other elements of this bill that are faulty. We think the scale of values the government has in trying to achieve restraint is all wrong. The government is restraining in the wrong places; there are places where restraint should be exercised which do not seem to have occurred to the government at all. Therefore, even with the assurance that clause 15 and subclause (4) of clause 16 will be removed, we still think the bill is a bad bill; bad positively in some of the things that are in it and bad in its failure to deal with some measures of restraint that ought to be before us at this time.
Therefore, on the second reading of the bill we shall be voting against it, and probably at further stages as well, but we are prepared to go along with the procedural suggestion made just now. I do join with my friend in welcoming the fact that clause 15 is to go, but I hope that before this session goes much further we may have greater parliamentary victories to celebrate than this one.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: BILL C-19-DELETION OF CLAUSE 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to reply only briefly on this motion in order to comment on the remarks of hon. members who have spoken to this point, particularly the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton. The government, in moving in this manner to take clause 15 out of the bill, is once again indicating its wish, wherever possible, to avoid the use of peremptory devices to put business to the question in this House. Of course, it is the over-all view of the government that after a reasonable time for debate the question ought to be put and an issue decided, rather than a constant prolonging of debate in this House.
The very prolonging of the debate on this issue rendered somewhat uncertain the timing of its application, and thereby makes sensible the separation of that particular clause from the rest of the bill. It is, however, the government's continued view that that clause and the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act should be proceeded with, and it will be a real advantage to have that clause standing separately and by itself in the bill so that the nature of the costs and the expenditures involved can be highlighted.
Hon. members opposite who sometimes show concern for the nature of expenditures may be asked to defend very specifically their opposition to a move which has in it the elimination of some long-standing payments which have led to high-cost transportation being used to accomplish things which could be accomplished with far less cost to the taxpayer. It will be our objective to highlight that. It is also true that the extra time involved will mean that the movements of grain, which were really assured for this winter, in any case, in the old, traditional pattern, will go on without any change at all in regard to the financial consequences.
December 6, 1976

In the meantime, discussions about the future movement of grain and the kind of conversations which could not take place so long as these artificial subsidies were in place will go forward, and the future will see the same kind of volumes of grain moved to markets with less total cost to the Canadian taxpayer and savings to that taxpayer, which is an objective all of us ought to share but which, of course, for various local and parochial reasons members opposite do not always share.
It will, therefore, be our intention to proceed with a separate measure; but we were able at this point in time to see the wisdom of dividing the bill rather than, as I say, using peremptory measures to bring to the question in this House an issue which has been before it for a long time, that very debate rendering uncertain the exact timing and implications for various parts of the industry and how the bill would operate.
This government has shown flexibility before this in other areas where, rather than move forward with measures to cut off debate, we have attempted in every reasonable way to have issues isolated and identified. We have done this once again. I will look forward to the separate debate on this matter. Of course I do not want to debate that particular issue at this point.

subsubtopic: BILL C-19-DELETION OF CLAUSE 15

Mr. Speaker, I apologize for having left the House at the start of the discussion but I was called to the phone on an urgent matter. I do not know whether stands were taken Friday in this regard, but I was told a while ago that the debate would be limited on this bill provided clause 15 is deleted.
We have argued twice about Bill C-19; I feel that is enough. We indicated to the government what we intended to do with regard to it and what we expected the minister to do, that is subdivide the bill so we could accept what is acceptable. For instance, we could take clause 2 of the bill on adult training and decide on that. Let us not mix this bill with feed grains or their subsidies. Clauses 3, 4 and 5 could easily be grouped together: they deal strictly with terminating the Company of Young Canadians. The same goes for Information Canada.
Let us discuss then decide upon, for instance, the clauses dealing with family allowances, as well as clause 12 on scientific research. I feel the government has already taken one small step in that direction simply by deleting clause 15 of the bill, to enable us to discuss the others; but it should go even further. I wonder what keeps it from presenting us with two more "small papers", thus allowing us to deal with each matter separately. That surprises me, even astounds me!

subsubtopic: BILL C-19-DELETION OF CLAUSE 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with some satisfaction that I speak on this closure motion today. When I spoke two weeks ago, I warned parliament that by putting in a statutory provision to repeal section 272 of a Railway Act the government unwittingly, I thought, was attacking the very foundations of our federal system. I asked the government at that time, two weeks ago, to please remove clause 15 and not be guilty of such a crime against the federal state. Apparently the government has yielded to that point of view, and I have to say, on behalf of those living in all parts of Canada who take pride that we were able to bring together a federal state since 1867, that we have not destroyed one basic foundation of that state.
But at the same time as I make that statement and review the debate of the last two weeks, I remember, as the fight went on in this House almost entirely by members of the official opposition and no one else on this fundamental question of protecting the right of the Atlantic provinces to be tied to the rest of Canada, that we received very little assistance from the members of the New Democratic Party. I say that flatly at this time. They will have to pay for that dereliction of duty.
The government is wise in backing off on this particular clause. It is wise because it is aware now that you cannot keep beating your head against the foundations of our federal system without causing some reaction from the people. The reason the government is withdrawing clause 15 is obvious. We have been running a filibuster here, as the hon. member for Fundy-Royal made very clear last week in a beautifully argued and coherent speech. He gave the legal background of all this protection we have given the Atlantic provinces. Now we are being asked to accept this motion by the government which allows it to bring in closure on the remaining clauses. That brings me to the second point of my remarks.
There are two specific issues in this bill. One is the view of the official opposition that clause 15 should be removed entirely because it has nothing to do with this type of bill and because it is a statutory protection for the people of the Atlantic provinces which originally goes back to the agreement dating long before confederation when we spoke of the interprovincial railway. That is the first issue.
The second issue is that the government was coming to the House and pretending that these various devices were a way of cutting down government expenditures. They were fooling the people that they would make cut-backs. The apparent nonsense of that was exposed in the Auditor General's report. We were able to use the arguments in the Auditor General's report. If you want to save money, cut out the business of pretending that the devices you brought forth in this bill are the only ways of restraining government expenditures. What will happen now is that clause 15 will be brought in in a separate bill and we will go back to debating the other issues
1690

December 6, 1976
Business of the House
as to whether these items are worth-while efforts in the restraint of public spending.
I want to conclude my remarks with a very simple and frank warning to the government. We know that the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act was an attempt to knock out the protection which the maritime provinces had under a statute of Canada that they would always be tied to this country by a railway or a water system, and that if there are any losses, we as Canadians across the country would help meet those losses. In this bill the government attacked that promise to the Atlantic provinces. We also know that very soon the government will be bringing in a bill to attack another great promise made to Canadians, to open up the west. That promise exists in a statute and is known as the Crowsnest pass rate. We feel in our hearts that the Minister of Transport and the government are trying to take away the western foundation of our federal union. If the government wonders why Canadians across Canada feel alienated, they should know that it is the result of their own mistakes.
They were wise to reconsider the repeal of section 272 at this time. I think the evidence we have is that the ministers are so busy flying up and down the country that they have no time to examine the legislation that is put before them and they allow this type of legislation to come to the House. They force those of us in the opposition who are aware of the implications of the issues before us to delay the passage of that legislation until somebody takes notice of the fact that we are delaying it. This is a victory for parliament. Those of us who debated this bill and pointed out these arguments to the government kept doing it until the government became aware of the fact that to get the bill through they would have to apply closure.
Personally, I do not believe that closure should be necessary in a democratic House of Commons at our stage of sophistication and development. The whole purpose of debate is to give us time to bring these matters to public attention. The issues brought out last week in the Auditor General's report and made known to the public by the media did not stop us from keeping up our battle here. The arguments and proposals put forward by the Auditor General should be dealt with, but we wanted the people of Canada to know there was a fundamental issue before us. The government did not want the people to know that. That is why they are deleting this clause from the bill.
I want to conclude my remarks by congratulating the government for coming to its senses. I hope the cabinet will have more time in the future to examine legislation which senior civil servants are putting before members of the government. We are the elected people of this country and we have a direct responsibility to the people. We are not run by a small group in the civil service whose idea it is to centralize everything. These beliefs are not only strongly held in Quebec but they are also strongly held in other parts of Canada. What has come out of this debate is that the Atlantic provinces knew they had friends in the official opposition from all parts of Canada. We are a united party on the issue of the federal union, and we do not try to destroy the connection.

The second fact that came to the attention of the people is that we in the official opposition are prepared to stand up and fight to force the government, by a filibuster, either to withdraw legislation or to amend it. They have surrendered and are withdrawing clause 15. I hope that when the Crowsnest pass rate fight starts, people from all parts of Canada and members from all parts of the House will join us in our fight to ensure that this tie with western Canada will not be destroyed by the government.

subsubtopic: BILL C-19-DELETION OF CLAUSE 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join my colleagues in expressing pleasure at the government's withdrawal of clause 15, action which at least for the time being grants a temporary reprieve with respect to the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act. The Minister of Transport indicated that this action was brought about by the responsible government party. I want to point out to him very clearly that it is an example, rather, of the government succumbing to an ever-watchful opposition doing its job in a very persistent and determined fashion. I do not know whether the government has indeed come to its senses, but I think it has a legislative program with which it has to proceed and, rightly or wrongly, it saw fit to propose this motion.
I should pay tribute to the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for St. Boniface. Last week I discussed this proposal with him and it seemed that he was the only person on that side of the House who was prepared to entertain such discussions. I believe that through his influence and because of his work with some of his senior cabinet colleagues that it was realized by the government members that we on this side of the House would not be prepared to succumb to any threats from the government.
The opposition to this bill from this side of the House is not new. It was clearly established last year when Bill C-87 was brought forth. As this party's House leader pointed out, extensive negotiations took place between the former president of the treasury board and the hon. member for Edmonton West. There was an exchange of correspondence in which we offered to trade off any one of the $74 million worth of cut-backs which we would have been prepared to support. No positive alternatives or suggestions emanated from the other side of the House, but we on this side offered some proposals to deal with the issue, followed by an exchange of correspondence. There was no further action after that.
The member of the Social Credit party brought out a very important fact, namely, that we are dealing with issues of such great importance that, as my friend the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain indicated, they tamper with the very fabric of confederation. Yet, this important measure is included in an omnibus bill.
You, Mr. Speaker, and your colleagues in the chair have had a great deal of difficulty throughout the debate on this bill in trying to determine what was or was not relevant to the bill. One of the reasons for this is that the bill represents a hodge-podge of legislation. We find here everything from the CYC to family allowances, to the grain stabilization legislation, to research and development, and to changes in the
December 6, 1976

Transportation Act. Surely, this should be a lesson to the government to stop the silly nonsense of bringing in omnibus measures which cover a variety of issues which should be dealt with singly so that members can address themselves to specific issues. Quite frankly, I hope the government will stop this practice of putting forward omnibus bills in the hope that one or two measures will slip through unnoticed.
In this case there was one specific issue which the opposition did not want passed, and it required the government to give in. As my colleague the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain pointed out, the repeal of the "at and east" rates represents an attack on the major fabric of confederation. Similarly, any change in the Crowsnest freight rate structure is an attack on the major fabric of our confederation.
We have a government and a Minister of Transport who, in the name of a selective user-pays philosophy, attempt to dismantle those things which bind us together. 1 do not downplay for a moment the significance of this issue to the agricultural industry. This would clearly have represented another slap in the face for agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture thought that this was a silly proposal, but it is quite obvious that he has now lost any effective clout he may have had at one time in the cabinet. Rather than diminishing support for the flour milling industry, which this particular provision would have done, we should be dealing with a proposal which would strengthen the flour milling industry. The fact of the matter is that the flour milling industry in this country has diminished rapidly and it is unable to compete on international markets. The government seems to want to destroy it completely.
The flour milling industry is very important to this country. It provides jobs, it is important to the maritime region and, quite frankly, I find it very cruel on the part of the government to propose a measure of this nature at a time when we need to create employment in high unemployment areas. Many government programs are being advanced to overcome the high unemployment problem in these particular areas. On the one hand, by bringing forward a measure such as this, the government would have exacerbated the unemployment problem while on the other hand the Minister of Manpower and Immigration has brought in programs which are intended to create employment. That certainly does not strike me as a smooth and efficient running of governmental operation.
The report of the Auditor General has clearly outlined the inefficiencies and problems in this administration, and if its books are as bad as the manner in which it proceeds with legislation, God help us.

obvious objection of the Minister of Transport in agreeing to this motion for the removal of the clause with respect to transportation. There has been considerable debate on the subject from all sides of the House and I do not think it was in the interests of a motion being accepted unanimously for the minister to say that while he is withdrawing this measure on this occasion because of certain circumstances, he is going to reinstate it.
I have never seen a minister more reluctant to change his mind than this minister. It is obvious that again, in this instance, he has been proved wrong by members of his own party, as well as by the effective opposition which has been put up by the official opposition and others in relation to this measure. But now the minister accepts these arguments with the statement that he is going to introduce this measure in some other manner.
This bill, and most omnibus bills which are brought in, indicate the weakness of the government and its inability to present legislation in a viable form. If it is necessary to bring in legislation in relation to a budget, I think the country understands the necessity to do that in terms of a number of items which are affected by budgets. This may be true with some of the legislation in this bill, but in the case of other parts of the bill, obviously there was no justification for bringing them in in this omnibus fashion. If an all-embracing bill is necessary, that seems to me to indicate the failure of the government to develop legislation which will stand on its own two feet. This has been the trade mark of this government for a number of years.
I was surprised by the argument of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain in which he took credit for what he believes to be a change in the whole fabric of our nation through transportation policy. He may be right that it has a tremendous effect, but I think he might have expressed it a little too strongly.
If there is unanimous agreement, it seems to me that probably the best course which could be embarked upon by all concerned would be to agree to pass this motion and go on with other matters, rather than the government taking the position that it had to do this today but is not committed to this course of action, and members on the other side saying they forced the government to do this. That does not seem to be any addition to the bill we have been discussing. It only highlights the weakness of the bill and, in my opinion, the inability of hon. members of the House to represent their constituents in an orderly fashion when there are a number of things we wish to support and a number we wish to oppose, and the bill gets bogged down in the discussion of individual factors without much hope of bringing about a major change in the legislation.
In fairness to itself, if the government really wishes to govern, in fairness to the opposition, if it wishes to be in opposition, and, much more importantly, in fairness to the people of this country so that they can sooner or later identify the issues of the day in this parliament, they should not be faced with bills they cannot understand which contain some-

That affects them, and in terms of restraint on the part of the government, they know what the Auditor General has pointed out about the tip of the iceberg in many departments. If the government really wants to practice restraint, if it wants to make constitutional changes in the direction our country may go through its transportation system, and if the government is really interested-and we know how interested it is-it would have its ministers present for the debate.
It has been very difficult for the ministers involved with these various restraints to force themselves to attend in the House for this debate. If this bill belonged to an individual minister and he had some responsibility for it, he would stay and put up some arguments; and if the government had a good case he would try to make that case. However, it is not possible for all the ministers involved with a conglomerate bill such as this to be in the House all the time to answer objections raised which relate to their departments.
Therefore, I think this type of legislation is bad legislation, and if there is to be an orderly use of the time of the House this type of bill should not be brought before us again.

The House resumed, from Tuesday, November 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-19, to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Holmes (p. 1393).

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this patchwork, band-aid approach to economic restraint of government expenditure in Bill C-19 is an inadequate, inept approach to the economic malaise of Canada. I agree with my colleague, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), that it is in reality an attack on the partners of confederation, inflicting further confrontary wounds on confederation not just in the sense of the rail situation but also the larger question of revenue sharing. Not only is our confederation strained and weakened by the excesses of our national government; it is strained and weakened both by its excessive spending and by its inept attempts at restraint.
While I am pleased that the provision regarding the railway subsidy has been removed, it is appropriate-and it should be clearly remembered-that the province I represent in this chamber agreed to enter confederation on the condition of rail transport connecting and serving the union of provinces. The threat of decreased rail service through the subsidy removal is a further attack on the very premises of western confederation. Before this ad hoc, band-aid approach is further pursued, other real alternatives must be examined.
In Canada today the provisions of Bill C-19 are but a small part of the endless bombardment of the tolerance level of confederation ethics. As a result Canadians spurred on by this type of legislation are beginning to question the larger basis of confederation. Canada has developed an unhealthy paranoia with its concern regarding Quebec's current and future role within confederation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) seems to see the solution through some excessive preoccupation and pursuit of an unworkable bilingualism program, blinded to the reality of the larger economic concerns-rail subsidy, family allowances, the aspirations of youth and the other social problems and concerns of Canada. We see personal and insidious grudge-match confrontation with the premier of Quebec, arrogant, ill-considered confrontation with the other premiers, and the vision of Macdonald's Canada begins to disintegrate amid petty parochialism and personal vendetta.
A new national perspective is needed now, not alternatives such as Bill C-19 that will weaken and further erode confederation, but courageous new vision to seek new proposals and understandings; to think with a freshness of the vigour and the vastness of our great country. The British North America Act has been, and continues to be, the cornerstone of our tradition
Restraint of Government Expenditures and our stability; and while no amendment formula has yet been achieved, Canada has continued to grow, to change and to evolve. New provincial boundaries have been established and adjusted regularly, even as recently as 1949. New responsibilities, like the environment, have been assumed and shared, and new revenue-sharing programs have been implemented with a flexibility not readily recognized in the BNA Act.
The potential of Canada, while currently somewhat dim and confused, is nevertheless as great as ever, but instead of playing with the same old hand-and Bill C-19 is a part of that same old, tired hand-it just may be the time to reshuffle the deck so the players can have a fresh look at a new hand.
While Canada is made up of a multiplicity of regions and cultures, it is my opinion that new, broad economic and cultural boundaries are beginning to evolve. Too often we consider only the regional culture of the French Canadian culture as contrasted to the English Canadian culture demonstrated by the traditions of Ontario. Any intelligent national perspective will show that if Quebec is a national cultural minority, in the same sense so are the maritimes a cultural minority, so are the prairies a cultural minority, so is British Columbia a cultural minority, and even patriarchal Ontario, as large as it is, exists as a minority amongst the other regions.
The maritime union study recognized the economic advantages of a regional unity, and Quebec, as a regional economic unit, has and continues to practice in this regionalized unit. Ontario, as the industrial heartland of Canada, has practised its own well-documented and pragmatic regional economic unitism since confederation. The prairies, combining its economic traditions as a major world bread basket, could well consider combining this long-term economic keystone with the currently depleting economic basis of oil, coal and potash. The isolation of British Columbia has built its own natural regional economic unit and pushed northward to reach outward to potential economic unity with the Yukon.
Canada unites naturally into five or six regions, not only culturally and economically but also geographically, in an obvious, broad manner. Politically, I cannot see a Canada with a special status for Quebec, any more than a Canada with a special status for British Columbia or any other individual province. I cannot see Quebec existing as a super province within confederation, further destroying an already out of balance interprovincial power structure.
Imagine, instead, five equal regional partners co-operating with a small but powerful central government in Ottawa. Consider a new revenue-sharing agreement where the provinces receive all of the revenue from resources as well as further tax points and, in return, deliver all services-health, welfare, education-more directly to the people of the region. Consider reorganizing equalization payments recognized by the central authority on the basis of direct payments to individuals according to income and need, rather than by region depending on their ability to govern. The potential and possibilities of the alternatives and combination of alternatives are limited only by lack of vision, tolerance and good will in the continued evolution of our great nation.
