Restraint of Government Expenditures
This is a period in Canadian history that cries out for common sense, flexibility, openness, moderation and tolerance. The centralists criticize the plan as further decentralization, while the decentralization see it as excessive centralization. My concept is not necessarily the final one to be adopted; let it stand, rather, as one of many open alternatives to be discussed with positive and progressive courage. No matter whether they cherish the vision of Sir John A. Macdonald's "Sea to Sea", the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker's "one nation", or W. A. C. Bennett's original "five regions concept", I urge today that the leaders of our provinces and nation, like our Fathers of Confederation, put aside their petty parochialism and vested interests and become the statesmen streamlining the stable roots of confederation into the modern and progressive vehicle to carry us swiftly and smoothly into our next 100 years of unity.
That attitude is not evident in the piecemeal, bandaid approach of Bill C-19. We need to adopt a fresh approach to the various regions of Canada. I say this bill deserves to be defeated, not because of the provisions it contains but because of its lack of vision. Ultimately the bill will be sent to committee, where it will be debated, after which it will return to this House. While the bill is being so debated, I hope we shall hear more about a vision of Canada predicated on the needs of the larger regions rather than on the objectionable legislation as put forward in Bill C-19.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was encouraged to listen to the speeches made on Bill C-19 by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). They spoke in support of the "at and east" rates, explained the difficulties which will be created for the east and the west and suggested ways of resolving such east and west difficulties. I suggest that the House owes those two hon. members a vote of thanks for their contributions. The essential purpose of bill C-19 is to restrain government spending, a subject with which the government is clearly unfamiliar.
Today I noticed that LIP grants for Kootenay West riding had been increased from $279,000 to last year's level of $608,000. In my view and the view of the Community Advisory Group, CAG, the money will be spent usefully in that it will help people in those pockets of unemployment in Kootenay West about which I am concerned. I am indeed grateful to the minister for this program; but, Mr. Speaker, I can think of at least one industry employing 90 people which has gone down the tube, so to speak, and which could have been helped. The industry in question manufactured and sold chain saws worldwide. Unfortunately, owing to a management misjudgment and dealings with a factoring firm, the company, Quadra Manufacturing, has met with financial disaster.
If only $200,000 of the extra LIP money granted to projects in Kootenay West could have been earmarked to help that industry, we could, instead of helping for three or four months people now unemployed, have guaranteed 90 employees steady employment for several years and an opportunity for that
[Mr. Wcnman.J
particular company to expand. I do not point the finger at ministers when we run into these difficulties, but what has happened clearly shows you the hidebound strictures placed upon ministers by senior civil servants, those insensitive, "go by the book" mandarins who run the government of this country.
What other industries are in similar circumstances? Surely a careful examination of business failures will reveal that some industries could be salvaged with a brief and not too massive injection of capital. Unfortunately, once a company is in receivership, government, the banks and just about everyone else turn their backs on the industry. And who is most affected by such business failures? The employee. The employee is affected in the long term and the investor in industry is affected in the short term, depending on his financial situation and how much he invested in the company.
I ask, how many businesses are now failing but could be saved if a program along the outlines I suggested were developed? How many jobs could be salvaged? I do not think the government has considered the question at all. I suppose hon. members opposite may say that such businesses can apply to the Federal Development Bank. Mr. Speaker, that high-risk organization is not about to open its doors to any company on the verge of receivership. I also ask, how many businesses are failing owing to the outflow of Canadian dollars to the United States? How can this government claim to be concerned about restraint if, through its actions and policies, it encourages the outflow of Canadian dollars to the United States?
For a change, let me refer to a success story, the operations of DREE in Quebec. I have often been critical of the DREE program and the amount of money injected by DREE into the province of Quebec. But an examination of the profile of development of secondary industry in Quebec indicates that the program has enjoyed a high measure of success. I suggest that if this government were truly aware of what is going on in the province, it might address its attention to that success story and emulate, with respect to all industries across Canada, what has been done by two or three people in the DREE organization in the province of Quebec. All Canadians, westerners and maritimers, alike, have been frustrated by noting the enormous volume of DREE money and tax dollars being poured into that particular province. But, Mr. Speaker, in all conscience I must give credit where credit is due. I challenge the minister responsible for DREE to go into the provinces, regardless of any federal agreement, and provide funds for industry. He does not need the agreement of the province concerned in order to do this. It is time he took such action.
I mentioned the outflow of Canadian dollars into the United States. This is another aspect of our financial position to which the government has not addressed itself. There is no question that Canada is faced with high labour costs. It can be argued that productivity here is lower than it is in the United States. Has the government looked into the reasons for these things, and addressed itself to the concern felt by the business commu-
December 6, 1976

nity with regard to the restrictions and amount of red tape placed upon manufacturers and producers?
Our party has declared that there will be a massive reduction in the federal government's involvement in the affairs of the small business community. Not too long ago a small industry in a community in my own riding wished to expand moderately-it was only a question of taking on six additional employees. But this would have brought the company under the wing of the AIB. Reports would have been required. The proposed expansion would have meant hiring another full-time employee and another part-time employee solely to handle reports to the AIB. I do not have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, what the decision was with respect to this expansion project. It was simply not worth it, and I could not agree more.
This is a classic example of the manner in which the government deals with small business. It has never accepted the fact that small business is the backbone of the nation. It might well be there are certain segments of the business community which are inefficient or counterproductive; no matter what injections of capital were provided, they would still fail, not because of labour costs but because of inefficiency and poor management. There is nothing that can be done to help this type of commercial enterprise.
To return to the point of debate concerning the outflow of Canadian dollars to the United States, I am particularly concerned with the cost of a number of Canadian products. I am thinking particularly of lumber, milled and finished, such as is produced in Kootenay West and in other parts of British Columbia. How is it that this lumber can be purchased much more cheaply in the United States than in Canada? The shallow answers I have received from the government to this question indicate that members over there would prefer to turn their backs on the situation and pretend it did not exist. They suggest the difference is due to transportation costs. Hogwash! When the mill is 20 miles down the road, how can they use that kind of phony excuse?
Then they say, "Well, it is volume buying." That answer is hogwash, too. In a great many cases the Canadian user with a mill nearby has the necessary market and is quite capable of buying in volume. I can think of one example involving a major undertaking to build senior citizens, homes. The contractor concerned went to Seattle, Washington, and brought back three flatbeds loaded with plywood sheets. After paying the duty, he was ahead one dollar a sheet-and you can get a whole lot of plywood aboard one flatbed. Thus, I discount the volume-buying theory.
If the reason for prices being higher in Canada than they are in the U.S. is that retailers here are charging excessive prices rather than working on a smaller profit basis, then the AIB is clearly failing in its function to apply a program of restraint and it is no wonder labour is frustrated as appearing to be the sole target of the board.
It is time the government got out into the country, talked to John Q. Public, listened to the opposition, grasped the fact that there is a problem out there and that there are a hell of a lot of dollars flowing into the United States, and that it will
Restraint of Government Expenditures take more than a 98-cent Canadian dollar to remedy the situation. So far, the government has shown itself hidebound in its responses. I have looked for some improvement, but I have come to believe that my hopes were in vain. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me a further opportunity to speak on Bill C-19.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure many of the things I am about to say have already been said by others. But the comments made by the Auditor General are so alarming that they bear repetition over and over again. We have found from past dealings with the government, both in the House and in committee, that at no time do members on the treasury benches pay attention to anything that is said only once. Never have they taken action on a suggestion that is made to them on only one occasion. However, I recall several examples of occasions on which constant repetition of a point over a period of weeks, months or even years eventually makes it sink into their thick skulls. The statement of the Auditor General to which I would direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, is this:
I am deeply concerned that parliament or, indeed, the government, has lost, or is losing, effective control over the public purse.
At no time in the history of this institution have we heard such a statement from an auditor general; and we have to remember that this gentleman is a non-partisan official responsible to parliament for examining the expenditure of any government which happens to be in power at a particular time. I suppose one could link this loss of control to which he referred with certain changes in the rules governing the method by which this institution considers government expenditure. A few years ago the estimates were studied in committee of the whole. At that time this House possessed the ability to extract answers from a minister as far as proposed expenditures were concerned. Ministers took this examination seriously. If a member asked a minister to explain why he was spending so much money on a particular item, he had to do so satisfactorily because if he did not questions could continue indefinitely, because Parliament at that time had the power to refuse to allocate funds to the government to carry on day to day business.
It was not so long ago that the greatest amount of damage to the rules was done, in 1969 or perhaps a little earlier, when estimates were taken out of the House and dates were set by which they were to pass. The net effect of this is very obvious when you compare the budget of the federal government in 1968 with the budget today. To refresh hon. members' memories, in 1968 the total budget was $10.8 billion. Today it is $42 billion, representing an increase of four times in a short period of eight years.
There is no doubt in my mind that this is clearly the result of ministers of the government no longer having to account to parliament for how they spend money. When questions are put to ministers during an examination of their estimates in committee, we witness the greatest display of stalling tactics one
1698

December 6, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures can imagine. Ministers give long, tortuous answers that do not provide any information, and sometimes even their advisers do the same thing.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, if the government is at all serious about wanting to show restraint in spending-and this bill is supposed to enable restraint of government expenditure to take place-that the government has really missed the boat. While this bill may indeed allow certain types of restraint to take place, in my view it is not of very great significance compared to bringing back to the House estimates for study. If the power and authority to study the estimates were given back to the House so we could hold up the proposed expenditures of the government until such time as all members of the House were satisfied that proper answers had been given by ministers about where expenditures were going to be made, this would be of significant benefit to Canada. Indeed, the government would have to indicate whether corrective action had been taken on former blunders pointed out in previous auditor generals' reports.
At this point I should like to make a suggestion, Mr. Speaker, though members on the other side pay very little attention to what we over here say; indeed, they sit there yacking away, not listening at all to what is said most of the time. I suggest that they should give serious consideration to giving the authority and power back to parliament to conduct a meaningful examination of the estimates each year when presented for study.
Other changes to the rules which in my view have resulted in less control over government expenditure are these. Standing committees are given the responsibility for studying estimates but, as I have already said, they have virtually no teeth at all. Government members are bent on speeding everything through, and opposition members on trying to make some sort of examination of the estimates, knowing full well that by a certain date all the spending proposals of the government will automatically pass no matter how hard they try to get explanations from the government or how much effort they put into trying to cut down some expenditures.
In standing committees in the past we have found that during the course of examination of estimates much information often comes to the surface which is worth thorough investigation of an impartial type. At the present time no committee has authority to conduct any kind of investigation unless and until a reference is made from the House itself; this, in effect, means the ministers concerned, which means the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself. So essentially we have a situation where the committees are virtually under the control of the Prime Minister.
If we uncover in committee evidence suggesting that some waste has taken place or that poor judgment has been shown in making expenditures, under today's rules the committee does not have authority to conduct a thorough and careful investigation into the matter. If we want to be serious about doing something to stop runaway expenditure on the part of the government, we must give standing committees the power to investigate without reference from the House, or from a

minister or the Prime Minister. I put this suggestion forward in a non-partisan manner. I believe this should be the case no matter which party is in power. If it were the case, I suggest we would have much less opportunity for waste or for dishonesty, perhaps, in the manner in which the government deals with public funds.
I do not think I should spend too much time reviewing many of the very glaring and wasteful expenditures described by the Auditor General, since we have already heard plenty of them. For example, there was the boat provided by the Canadian Commercial Corporation for CIDA, eventually costing nearly $1 million and which was rejected by the recipient country because it was an unstable vessel. There was the waterfront property in Vancouver that was leased at five times the rent that the previous tenant paid, with government having no visible use at all for the property. There was the Atomic Energy of Canada Limited expenditure of $15 million; and the unexplained revelations regarding Polymer and a whole host of other things. All of these could be subjects for investigation by committees, and this they could do if they had the right without restriction being placed on them in the form of a reference from the House itself. In my view, in the long run the effect of such authority vested in committees would prove very beneficial to the country as a whole.
I also want to touch on the subject of freight rates. I know it has been raised in this chamber on many occasions and was discussed at the western opportunities conference called by the Prime Minister a number of years ago. Anyone who has any interest in freight rates is already fully aware of the problems. As I have already said-and it is worth repeating because perhaps someone on the government side will listen-to hold this country together it must be recognized by our political leaders in the federal government and in each province that transportation and communications are the key. Indeed, they were the key that was largely responsible for bringing this country together in the first place. This is how our federal system was developed. The key to making the system work was recognition that wherever one lived in this country, whenever areas were developed and new land opened up equal treatment from a transportation point of view would be afforded. Everyone was to have access to adequate transportation on facilities in order to transport goods to market and to bring in whatever supplies were required to run businesses and agricultural enterprises.
Yet today, Mr. Speaker, it is transportation inequity and remoteness from communication which make our northern people so hostile to those of us who live in the south. Indeed, it is also inequity in transportation that creates a good deal of hostility among westerners and maritimers alike toward central Canada where freight rates are extremely discriminatory. I have the rates before me so as to illustrate in a little more detail what I mean. The fact is that freight rates are set up in such a way that manufacturing industries are encouraged to establish in central Canada, and discouraged from establishing in the western part of the nation or in the Atlantic provinces.

Let us take, for example, the cost of shipping a live steer from Saskatoon to Toronto or Montreal. The total shipping cost of a 1,000-pound animal is $30.92. If that animal were slaughtered and dressed in Saskatoon and all of the parts obtained for sale; that is the meat and various by-products were shipped to Montreal, the total cost would be $37.24. We have a difference of $6.32 per animal. If the animals are shipped live, there is a saving in transportation of $6.32 per animal. If you multiply that by several thousand animals, you will see it is a fairly significant difference. This difference favours the slaughtering and processing taking place in either Toronto or Montreal. I am sure that is a reflection of the fact that we have a rather lopsided House of Commons. I am not suggesting representation by population is not a good thing-I think it is the only way to go-but we know also that the majority of constituencies in this country are within the two major central provinces, namely, Ontario and Quebec.
This kind of shortsightedness on the part of government in power has resulted in discrimination in many areas, but transportation is the most obvious one. This is discrimination against the weak, and in my view is not a very charitable approach by government. Because there are fewer people in the west and in the maritimes the majority is able to abuse and take advantage of the relative weakness of these people in terms of numbers.
Let me refer to another example, that of rapeseed. When rapeseed is crushed you have various components; you have 38 pounds of rapeseed oil from 100 pounds of rapeseed, and 62 pounds of meal. The oil is shipped at a rate of 41.8 cents, and the meal at 23.5 cents. The rate is 59 cents from Thunder Bay to Montreal and represents a total cost of 93 cents per 100 pounds moving from west to Central Canada. If the rapeseed were crushed in Montreal and the product shipped in the other direction, the cost would be 67.5 cents per 100 pounds. This represents a difference of 25.5 cents per 100 pounds in favour of processing the rapeseed in Montreal, or a difference in freight rates of some 30 per cent. There is no explanation for that outside of its being plain, ordinary, bald-faced discrimination by virtue of a larger number of people in one part of the country and a government without the guts to speak up for all parts of the country and simply catering to the central part where the votes are.
The government should have the guts to explain the situation or stand for equity for all parts of the country. After all, we are all Canadians and we must be concerned about each other's economic and social welfare. Those are the comments I wanted to make in respect of freight rates. We also know that these freight rates have over the past 100 years resulted in obvious inequities. They have resulted in manufacturing industries being centred almost exclusively around the major population areas of Ontario and Quebec. I am prepared to suggest that this in large part is the result of the kind of freight rate structure we are experiencing in this country.
Let me move on to the matter of closure of rail lines to which this government has dedicated itself. There have been
Restraint of Government Expenditures
hearings held around the country and certain lines have already been closed or abandoned.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I thought you were in favour of restraint.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I am sorry, I did not hear what the hon. member said. I will give him a chance to speak when I have finished, and that will not be too much longer.
We have a situation today in which the unity of our country is in great danger. Transportation is a very important factor, not only in respect of the economic development of all parts of the country but also in respect of the development of unity in this nation. Certain rail lines were never completed. It is my suggestion that some line connections should be made. The hon. member opposite suggested that I should be in favour of restraint. My suggestion that some rail line connections be completed is in line with restraint, because this would cut down the cost of transportation in certain areas and in the long run would contribute to the greater development of these areas and the over-all economy of the nation.
Rather than established lines being abandoned, we must complete the construction of certain connecting lines in order to make northern rail services economic. Many settlers were induced to homestead on the prairies by the promise of rail connections by the CPR or the CNR. The Frenchman's Butte line running in an east-west direction has never been connected to another line running from Elk Point to Heinsberg. As a result, there has never been the efficiency that this line was supposed to have achieved. It seems to me we should be looking at ways of correcting these discrepancies in rail line construction in order to achieve greater transportation efficiency.
One can easily see there can be no sound and progressive development of the rich mineral and agricultural potential of northern Saskatchewan and Alberta without a viable transportation framework in this area. This is particularly true in that area of northwestern Saskatchewan and northeastern Alberta which takes in my own constituency. The only impediment to this framework is a rail line connection in the area running from Grand Centre and Cold Lake to a point in Saskatchewan in the vicinity of Meadow Lake. There is no doubt in my mind that if this connection were made, the cost of transportation in these areas would be substantially reduced. In view of the rapid development taking place in northern Alberta in relation to the sands, such a connecting line would substantially reduce the cost of shipping manufactured goods in from central Canada. This, in turn, would reduce the cost of constructing the tar sands plants, a cost that we all know is extremely high at the moment.
That brings me to an area in which I think the government is showing a good deal of shortsightedness. I refer to the development of the tar sands. In May, 1976, some six months ago, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) released a statement called "An Energy Strategy for Canada." In that paper he seemed to be taking the position
80005-40%

December 6, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures that our only hope for energy self-sufficiency-and we all agree we should be aiming for that, and can achieve it-was in exploration for conventional oil all over this country and perhaps in other parts of the world. He suggested that $40 billion would be invested in conventional oil and only $5.6 billion would be expended on tar sands plants.
I think we all agree that some conventional exploration is necessary because there are still deposits to be found, but we might compare the cost of that kind of exploration to the cost of extraction plants in the tar sands region where we know the resource is, where we know what the cost is to take it out, and where we know the cost of the plants. It seems to me there would be much more logic in taking a greater interest in the development of the tar sands.
I might elaborate on that a little. The requirements of this country are something like two million barrels a day, to use rough figures. We are producing about that much and are exporting a little less than half of it. Therefore, we import from offshore sources, to make up the difference. The price of offshore oil has developed in such a way that a hardship has been created for our country. It seems to me that if the government had enough vision into the future, it would be possible for us to be self-sufficient within one or two decades from now. This, however, would require a plan of action which must be implemented immediately and must be proceeded with at a fairly rapid rate.
I have mentioned the fact that we require something in the order of two million barrels a day. We also know there is one plant in operation at Fort McMurray which is producing
65.000	barrels a day, and that there is another under construction which will be completed in a year or two which will produce 125,000 barrels a day. So if we are looking only to replace the one million barrels a day that we are importing now, simple arithmetic suggests that perhaps nine plants would achieve self-sufficiency under today's requirements.
We know that our requirements are going up all the time, and projecting increasing needs it is still rather obvious that self-sufficiency could be easily achieved by fairly speedy development of the tar sands area. There are some 2,000 or
3.000	workers in the tar sands region now constructing a plant. It took a number of years to assemble the people and the equipment capable of constructing such a plant. At the moment, with the lack of interest the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is showing, it appears that there will not be another plant ready to go into construction when the present one is completed. This means that the crew and the equipment will disperse, and therefore contribute to the increased cost of another plant when construction begins.
So if we are concerned about expenditures in the area of energy production and considerable savings, then we should be interested enough to ensure that the new plant is started at least as soon as we would be required to keep that crew and equipment working without a break. Unless we take such action and adopt a policy which calls for rather speedy development of the tar sands, the prospect of our having self-suf-
(Mr. Yewchuk.]
ficiency by the end of the next decade or two is almost non-existent.
If we want to have self-sufficiency in respect of oil and petroleum by the end of the next decade, if we want to avoid the kind of prices we will be forced to pay for the imported product, and if this government is serious about trying to show restraint in respect of expenditures, then the government must be concerned about the situation on a long-term basis rather than the short-term basis. The government must be concerned about long-term savings for the taxpayers of Canada in this regard.
Another area relating to energy production is Petro-Can. This is a Crown corporation with a proposed initial budget of some $l'/2 billion. I shall not spend too much time today arguing whether Crown corporations are more efficient or whether private corporations are more efficient in producing energy; suffice it to say that private corporations have been in this business for a long time and have done a pretty good job of providing Canada and, indeed, the world with required energy resources. We all know that the private corporations have been pretty good taxpayers in this country and that the public purse takes reasonably good advantage of those taxes.
On the other hand, not only would it cost $ 1 !6 billion to get the Crown corporation off the ground, but once it is off the ground it will not be a taxpayer. As a matter of fact, it may well continue to be a drag on the public purse. In a time of restraint, it seems to me this is another area at which the government should take a serious look, particularly in terms of this $ 1V6 billion investment that is required to get this corporation off the ground and in terms of the fact that this corporation will not be paying taxes and, indeed, will not offer us any tax relief.
One other area on which I wish to touch briefly is that of scientific and medical research. I do not think there is a person in the world who would argue about the value of research. I can think of many examples where a certain amount of money that was expended in respect of the development of a new product, whether it be a drug, a new machine or a computer, resulted in manifold savings in terms of dollars. I will use the development of polio vaccine as an example. We have compared the cost of the research in respect of immunization with the cost of looking after polio patients who require iron lungs and long terms in hospital involving such medical and pursing care. The investment, in terms of research and development, in respect of polio vaccine represents a saving of 100 to 1. For every $1 invested, $100 has been saved. I do not say that all research produces this kind of spectacular result in terms of savings, but we know that in respect of medical research, with which I am most familiar-and I think this would apply to other scientific research-the savings ratio is 20 to 1. For every $1 invested in research for the discovery of new treatment, and so on, we have a saving of $20.
We have a government which seems to be totally incapable of comprehending the long-term savings which accrue from
December 6, 1976

active participation in a vigorous research program. We in Canada, for example, spend about one-sixth of what is spent by the United States, Holland, Sweden or Germany, on a per capita basis, on medical research. For some strange reason the former minister of science and technology, the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury), seemed to think we did not have to have our own research programs, because through the charity of other countries which have such programs we could have the information free of charge.
That kind of approach is nothing short of despicable. Canada not only has a responsibility to the world for achievements in science, but it has a responsibility to its own citizens in that respect. If we talk about restraint, let me point out that you achieve long-term restraint in spending through research. Until the government accepts that as its basic philosophic approach, I am afraid that the band-aid measures proposed in Bill C-19 will have virtually no effect in restraining government spending.
Before concluding my remarks I should like to refer to the matter of national unity and the credibility of this government so far as its intentions are concerned. On the one hand it says it wants to restrain spending, and on the other hand it is not exercising its own recommendation. It has asked labour to restrain its demands for wage increases to about 8 per cent, yet its own increase in this year's budget amounts to around 16 per cent. The people of this country find it almost impossible to believe what this government says. I have some examples of that. Less than a year ago, in December, 1975, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said:
The new kind of society we will need to create in response to the new economic circumstances in which we are living here in Canada and throughout the world ... The free market system is not working and never really existed .. . The government must use controls to get institutions and people to change.. . We haven't been able to make even a modified free market system work in Canada ... It is the government's duty to intervene when necessary to stimulate employment, to redistribute income, to promote conservation, productivity and an adequate supply of the things we need-
Now, 11 months later, the Gallup polls are showing that this approach by the Prime Minister created a certain amount of suspicion towards his policies. So, in the throne speech he said:
Canada's traditional reliance on individual enterprise as the mainspring of economic activity ... Prices to be determined by the free play of market forces.
What we have here is an example of the attitudes that have been portrayed by virtually everyone in the cabinet over the past six or eight years. On the one hand they suggest that they will take a certain policy direction, and on the other they make a totally opposite statement several weeks or months later. Another example of that is the wage and price control program itself. In 1974 the Prime Minister campaigned, saying that wage and price controls would not work. Then, a year later, the government brought them in itself. The moral of all this is that the government should show some restraint in talking out of both sides of its mouth. If it did, perhaps it would show a tendency to restrain spending. People should know what the government stands for and they should be able to believe what the government says. If that were the situation, there would be much less unrest in the country and perhaps a
Adjournment Motion
greater desire on the part of labour and industry to co-operate in restraint in a general way.

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Goodale), and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), while succumbing to the pressures of the opposition on Bill C-19, particularly on clause 15, finally agreed today to withdraw the clause. However, almost in the same breath both those hon. members made sure to point out to the House that the government would be introducing the same measure, namely, the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act, in another bill.
We witness a great deal of arrogance in the House emanating from the government side, but for the Minister of Transport to withdraw this clause from the bill and in almost the same breath indicate to the House that he will be bringing in legislation containing the same measure is the absolute height of arrogance. The minister must have missed the whole point of this debate. The objections from this side of the House have centred around clause 15. They have been outlined by speaker after speaker on this side of the House and the objections have been supported by various farm organizations, by the flour milling industry, by the grain elevator companies and by many people associated with the movement of grain.
As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) pointed out, and as I pointed out earlier, section 272 of the Railway Act is part of the very fabric that holds this country together. In my view, it is destructive for the Minister of Transport to have embarked upon a policy of a selective user-pay concept to bring about such a measure at this juncture in our history.

December 6, 1976
Merchant Marine

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO REVIVE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of reviving the Canadian Merchant Marine and applying recommendations of the Darling Report.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as you are no doubt aware, hon. members are not surprised to see me rise to take part in the debate on the notice of motion I myself put before the House. I do hope, Mr. Speaker, this is the last time I shall rise to discuss the Canadian Merchant Marine. Some are annoyed to hear me repeat speeches I have been making for about 15 years but, Mr. Speaker, though some think that we need a merchant marine strictly to help out our shipbuilding yards, I say not so because last week-and I must take this opportunity to congratulate him for it-the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) came to my home to announce that the policy has been changed with regard to aiding the shipbuilding industry, that is the 13 per cent subsidy that applies to that industry.
That program, as we know, Mr. Speaker, used to apply solely to the construction of completely Canadian ships but as of today it will also apply to the renovation and refit of Canadian ships. So it is a matter of helping our shipyards which are now in a very precarious position. I am not speaking here only of Lauzon and the Davie Shipbuilding but also of Halifax, Vancouver, of Marine Industries Ltd. which now has orders to last it till the end of 1979.
In the motion, the government is requested to apply the recommendations of the Darling report as soon as possible.
Perhaps I should give a summary of the Darling report which, in fact, recommends the establishment of a Canadian merchant marine, and for several reasons. Here I have to digress and recall that the new premier of Quebec, Rene Levesque, came in my constituency and visited the shipyards employees during the electoral campaign. He came perhaps to promise the establishment of a Quebec merchant marine. I wonder then if Mr. Levesque knew the recommendations in the Darling report. Why do we hesitate? And this is the question I am asking of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Roy). Why do we hesitate? Maybe it is because Canada is not such a large country after all. But when I see Mr. Levesque, now premier of the Province of Quebec, promising the establishment of a Canadian merchant marine, I wonder if his speech to the employees was really serious.
But, what are we to do? After the elections of November 15, I said: "There they are, they have to govern, they made promises and they will have to account for them to the public at the next election. Therefore, they will be judged by their
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
actions. The Parliamentary Secretary may tell me: We are still considering the recommendations of the Darling Report. But for several years, studies have been conducted not on costs but on the advisability of establishing a Canadian Merchant Marine.
As far as I am concerned, I have not yet seen anything to convince me that the government is seriously taking the Darling Report recommendations, which happen to suggest a positive attitude towards problems related to the establishment of a Canadian Merchant Marine, by strengthening authority, by giving real powers to a department or an agency whose main responsibility would be to establish a Merchant Marine, and to set up its various stages. I am not pressing for the establishment of a Canadian Merchant Marine any more than other hon. members do, nor am I advocating, as Mr. Levesque says, that: "The day after the separation of Quebec, we shall have a merchant marine." It is not so. I am taking part in this debate and asking the government to implement the recommendations of the Darling Report because I want us to put an end to the present confusion and powerlessness, because I am still wondering who must make the decisions. Is it the Treasury Board or the Department of Transport? Is it the cabinet as a whole or a committee of the cabinet? I dare hope that today we shall have some answers from the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Roy). So why do we speak of "real powers", of "taking initiatives"? That is what the Darling Report says.
At present, as I said a moment ago, there is no legislation or direct policy. No administrative guideline says whether we shall have a merchant marine or not. I already took part in several debates to ask the government to be more alert or at least head the recommendations of a report which was submitted to the government on February 5, 1975. Well then, are we going to get any guidelines or be told that this report is no longer relevant, that we need another one? What do we need? I am looking forward to these statements, I know several hon. members plan to take part in the discussion of this issue which is of great significance not only to our shipyards, but also to the reputation of Canada. We are one of the few countries with a such long coastlines and yet no merchant marine.
We have everything we need to develop one, Mr. Speaker, we have the equipment in our shipyards-and we all know the efforts made by many shipyards throughout the country to invest huge amounts of money to increase their productivity and enter the world shipbuilding market. Very interesting programs have been applied to assist ship exports. But our shipyards, either Marine Industries, Halifax, Burrard or any Canadian shipyard, are running out of orders and this is why we need some answers.
A coalition was formed recently to once more raise the issue of the establishment of a merchant navy as recommended in the Darling Report. I therefore urge the government, not to indicate that tomorrow they will accept those recommendations, and that tomorrow everything will be done to establish a merchant navy, but at least to state the policy they intend to put forward to bring about these recommendations.

It would be very important that a time frame be specified, as a five year period for instance. We should proceed by stages, as was done in the case of domestic shipping in Canadian waters, for which a five year period was provided, I do not ask that this be necessarily done over such a five year period, but the government should indeed make definite commitments to create jobs not only in our naval yards, but also on the ships themselves that will ply the oceans. This could help shipbuilding and Canadian trade. This was the area on which the Darling Commission put particular emphasis: helping Canadian trade, balance of payments and international image.
As I said in this House a number of times, public opinion is already sold on this. I therefor hope that it is one of the last times, if not the last, that I rise in such a debate. Public opinion, shipowners and media are already sold on this. They are well aware of the advantages and prerequisites, because there will no doubt be prerequisites to be establishment of such a merchant navy. First of all, we must consider all the consequences. We must examine the costs as well as the problems we shall be faced with, because we have obligations to meet. I am aware that we very often sell wheat to the Russians. In the contracts they sign, they will demand that their ships be used for shipments from Canada, thereby creating jobs for their merchant marine.

. . . The government was specifically requested to accelerate order placing for the building of coast guard boats and fishing patrol vessels. Canadian shipbuilders. The text is very long and I do not intend to read it all. If the hon. member's motion were adopted, the impact on Canadian shipyards would be tremendous. The hon. member for Levis indicated the precarious position in which Canadian shipyards may find themselves. If I were from the river ports, I would not cry too much; they, at least, have good prospects for the next two or three years. I know that shipyard difficulties are worldwide; yet we stand to lose, for the first time in 200 years, workers capable of engaging in the entire range of skilled shipbuilding activities. Once we lose them, we shall never regain them. We cannot afford to retrain other workers; in any event, I do not know where we would find them. Therefore, once we lost these workers they will be gone for good and we shall see no more like them probably for a generation. It would do that if the government would show a positive attitude with respect to the Darling report and implement two or three simple suggestions. Irving, on the east coast, and others, we would be going a long way to re-stablishing the Canadian merchant fleet. We must make clear our attitude with respect to the coastal trade of Canada. In that connection, I was personally pleased to note that the minister undertook to bring the maritime code back to the House without those provisions dealing with the coastal trade. I hope we can deal with the matter quickly, possibly before we adjourn for Christmas, so that we can deal with the other parts of the bill in the new year. Hopefully, we shall receive the views of those engaged in the coastal trade before the bill receives final approval next spring.
We must also consider the matter of excessive pilotage fees and overly stringent regulations. I say this because a foreign master regularly calling at the port of Halifax no more needs a pilot than he needs the man in the moon. Indeed, we run a grave risk by always insisting on a pilot. The winter before last, during the so-called energy crisis, a tanker stood off outside the entrance of Halifax harbour because there was a pilots' strike. During this time, probably one of the most competent masters with respect to the port of Halifax stood by, afraid in case a change of wind would make the tanker broach or run aground on the rocks off the island which was lying close to the ship. I say that a competent master could have sailed her in without difficulty. The port is a safe one. I therefore say that we must reconsider our overly stringent regulations, the matter of excessive pilotage fees, current financing policy and tax policy. I mention tax policy because of the hesitancy of Canadian entrepreneurs who but for our tax policies would be willing to participate in a Canadian merchant marine.
Let me touch on one or two areas of concern. I should like to see the subject matter of the motion referred to committee. Let me say at once that at one time ships involved labour-intensive operations; now they are capital intensive, something one should bear in mind considering present-day fuel prices and the worldwide competition among shipyards. It is interesting to note that as of 18 months ago Canadian crew wages were 10 per cent lower than those paid to United States crews, about 9 per cent higher than those paid to U.K. crews, 15 per cent higher than Greek rates, 10 per cent more than German rates, and on a par with Norwegian and Swiss rates. Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to entend my congratulations to the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) for presenting this motion, and to the hon. members for Dart-mouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) and for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) for taking part in this debate during private members' hour.
Mr. Speaker, I would first refer to the statement of the hon. member for Levis, who was worried about whether his motion annoyed hon. members and expecially the Department of Transport. Let me tell the hon. member for Levis that his concern is ill-founded. The situation is changing all the time and we take a close look at all changes in world shipping.
The hon. member for Levis said that promises were made during the Quebec elections concerning the Quebec merchant marine. For his information and that of the hon. member running at that time for the Quebec provincial leadership, I would simply like to quote figures concerning the cost of government intervention in shipping. The study of the U.S. Commerce Department entitled Foreign Maritime Aids, shows that it is very costly to subsidize a fleet. For example, in 1972, the United Kingdom subsidized its shipping industries at the rate of $550 million, over and above added value tax exemptions worth some $37 million. The hon. member for Roberval said, if I read him right, that the merchant marine even made some savings possible, and that it was not so to be considered an expense but an investment. I would like to draw to the attention of the hon. member the situation in Japan where the government subsidized its shipping industries at the rate of about $500 million a year, and allocated in 1973 $278 million for the purchase of ships for Japanese nationals.
If I may once again refer to the study on the importance of the merchant marine for Canada, I am convinced that, as the hon. member said, Canada has a real advantage when it comes to shipping because of its Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic coast lines. And that situation serves it quite well commercially since Canadian importers and exporters have several options open to move the goods they control. Mention should also be made of the presence of the Great Lakes in the middle of the continent; they represent a real inland sea and assure a shipping link essential to the existence and the development of the centre of the country. So it seems somewhat paradoxical that in spite of such a favourable geographic location Canada should not have a more sizeable fleet of ships plying international waters. However we do have an important fleet on the Great Lakes and the west coast.
December 6, 1976

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to continue the history of the merchant marine but I would like to recall certain economic factors showing the significance of transportation and give a few figures on the Canadian shipping trade. I would like to indicate that in 1974 the following tonnage was registered in Canadian ports: 67 million tons on the import side, and 117 million tons on the export side. So the total international trafic was 184 million tons in 1974. Of that total 74 million tons represented our shipping trade with the United States-40 per cent. In the early 50s the Canadian international trafic was only about 70 million tons.
Those few figures illustrate rather well the growth in our external trade but also show our dependence on foreign fleets handling our business. In 1974 Canadian registered ships moved 44 million tons of freight-24 per cent of the total- but the majority of that freight was to or from the United States. It must be pointed out on the other hand that most foreign registered ships belonged to industrialized countries and Canadian allies. So the risks of an abrupt and violent upset in our shipping trade are rather limited.
I will now deal with world changes. It is unlikely that the policy of non-interference and free competition carried on by Canada since World War II will continue much longer in view of world wide disruptions in shipping.
More and more, countries all over the world give nearly unconditional support to their merchant marine. Some want prestige, others regard this as on opportunity to stock foreign currencies which are required for their balance of payments, while others want to increase their national security. At the same time, protective measures are taken, and there is some talk about sharing the shipping among trading countries, and bilateral or multilateral maritime agreements are being considered. the most significant of these developments is probably the proposal to the United Nations for the setting up of an operational code concerning shipping lines operating whithin the framework of conferences, which would divide trade in the following manner: 40 per cent for the exporting country, 40 per cent for the importing country and 20 per cent for the third country. Canada may easily be affected by such developments and could find itself restricted by foreign fleets which could increase their freight while our shippers would be unable to adopt counter measures.
I would now like to come back to what the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) had to say about the Darling Report. Recognizing the vulnerable position of Canada in the maritime sector that I mentioned the Department of Transport asked Mr. Darling to report on the maritime situation in Canada and to recommend action. Following his researchs which were carried out during the summer of 1974, Mr. Darling submitted a report which recommends the need for Canada to take a more positive stand on shipping and to recognize the necessity for a better formulation of a Canadian policy concerning international shipping; along the lines the hon. member for Levis mentioned in his speech. Contrary to what many people may think, the Darling Report does not necessarily urge the
Merchant Marine
establishment of a Canadian merchant marine, but recognizes that certain national interests go beyond the traditional commercial context and that certain problems cannot be solved within a market economy.
Mr. Darling does not reject the possibility of developing a merchant marine as it is a possible option, but he does not suggest a major marine reconstruction. I wish also to mention a few achievements in that field. I shall come back to a point raised by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) concerning costs. I think it is too early to evaluate the possibilities of major changes but several factors indicate that the traditional differences between Canadian and foreign costs could continue to decrease. For instance, the industry becomes increasingly capital intensive and the cost of manpower represents an always decreasing part of the total cost. On the other hand, the action of international sea farers unions toward wage parity for the crews of different countries should help a nation like Canada become more competitive than we are now. Those developments are international but here in Canada, trade unions have shown a very positive and constructive attitude regarding the expansion of our marine activities. However this outlook should be evaluated on a rather long term and the move toward a larger Canadian fleet should be progressive and possibly rather slow as required by the present economic situation.
I shall mention a very precise aspect, which is the M. V. Arctic vessel, one of the most concrete aspects of Canadian interest in the marine field. I want to speak about the icebreaker M. V. Arctic which is under construction in the Canadian shipyard of Port Weller in Ontario. This vessel will cost about $40 million and will be ready by May 1978. A consortium of private corporations supported by strong government participation will ensure the operation of that vessel. We hope that this prototype will demonstrate the economy of operation of that type of vessel and will be the start of a very strong Canadian presence in Arctic waters. A Canadian marine activity represents a support and supplement to the mining and economic activities in this developing area.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude my remarks on the same concrete note. I would like to point out that many recommendations of the Darling report have already been considered by the government and that through the Shipping Advisory Board it has been possible to co-ordinate federal activities in shipping. We are more and more inclined to deal with countries whose policies have direct effects on our external trade. Canadian shipping companies operating internationally now can submit their views to Ottawa on their new role in a new structure.
As I mentioned earlier, the building of the M.V. Arctic and the efforts made to restrict coastal shipping to Canadian vessels are true indications of the government's will to consolidate the position of Canadian shipping operators. However it would not be advisable to build a merchant fleet without being sure that Canada would derive direct or indirect benefits. The fantastic costs of government assistance require great care and point to the need for a sound analysis of all element of our

As I indicated before the dinner adjournment, Mr. Speaker, one of the primary reasons that we on this side of the House took objection to Bill C-19 was the application of the selective user pay concept which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has adopted in terms of overhauling the transportation policy, and in so doing he has threatened to destroy the basic fabric which holds this nation together. In that connection I am very pleased to see the Minister of Transport in the House. We would welcome his participation in this debate.
It is interesting to note that today when we are debating Bill C-19 dealing with section 272 of the Railway Act we have been informed that the Snavely report has been tabled, a significant report in which I am sure everyone connected with grain transportation will be interested. For those hon. members who may not know what the Snavely report is, let me explain that the Snavely Commission was established to look into the cost of the movement and handling of grain.
As pointed out in the press release of the Minister of Transport today, its primary task was to identify the total costs and revenues to the railways of transporting grain under temporary conditions. Its second task was to evaluate railway costing practices, using the Canadian Transport Commission cost order as a base, and to identify and review any related grain costing issues.
I think that all hon. members will look upon this document as being very important in dealing with the issue of determining what is and what is not a fair rate to be applied to the movement of grain. It seems to me that when we discuss any freight rate changes for the movement of grain, and when we engage in any sort of informed or intelligent discussion or debate upon the revision of any freight rate structure in this connection, it is of the utmost importance to have this information before us. I have not had an opportunity to assess or study the findings of this report. Only the minister has this information at his fingertips.
The minister indicated today that he will be proceeding with the introduction of a bill which would in fact repeal Section 272. He went on to point out that then we will be in a position to deal with this issue on its particular merits, and we will have all the cost data available and we will be able to determine exactly what it would cost the Canadian taxpayer. I will welcome that opportunity, but up until now we have not really had that information, and the Snavely Commission will certainly provide us with the kind of data I think we require to look into this and to assess the impact of any restructuring of freight rates in connection with the movement of grain.
The thrust of Clause 15 of Bill C-19 to me is another slap in the face of agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has pointed out in many speeches-I do not know of any other minister who makes as many speeches as the Minis-
December 6, 1976

ter of Agriculture, but I had the occasion this week end to read about a dozen speeches he made throughout the country in the last week or ten days-that only 2 per cent of the federal budget is allocated to agriculture. He points out that in the EEC something like close to $9 billion is being allocated to the development and maintenance of the viability of the agricultural industry. He points out that only 6 per cent of our population is associated with the direct production of agricultural products, and yet this 6 per cent generates some $5 billion worth of direct business activity in terms of the purchase of machinery, the purchase of repair parts, tires, fuel, etc. Surely that is a very important industry in the over-all economic picture of this country.
The minister pointed out further-and 1 agree with him in this connection-that some 45 per cent of our gross national product is related to agriculture and other activities ancillary to the agricultural industry. I see the parliamentary secretary in the House. I know he agrees with me, and he should, because I am quoting his own minister. Having said that, one would think that hon. members opposite would be rising in their places and defending the interests of agriculture, but what this bill is doing is destroying a very important element of the agricultural industry and an industry which is associated very closely thereto. Rather than withdrawing the special freight rate which Clause 15 undertakes to do, it seems to me that the government should be considering ways and means of assisting that particular industry, namely, the flour milling industry.
I pointed out earlier this afternoon when I participated in the debate on the motion which was introduced by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Goodale) that the opposition to this legislation did not spring up overnight. The opposition to this legislation has been well known and well documented for a long period of time.
I recall that on March 19 I raised a question in this House relating to the impact which the removal of the transportation subsidy on grain and flour shipped from our eastern coast ports would have on this very important industry. It was a policy decision at that time which I thought was wrong, and which I considered should be reversed. In responding to the question I advanced at that time the Minister of Agriculture left the impression that the flour milling industry was indeed a dying industry for export purposes. He implied that as far as we as a nation are concerned it was better for us to ship the raw product in the form of wheat rather than to worry about the processing of it in the form of flour. It is this sort of shallow attitude in the government which I find very disturbing. It is an attitude which has led to what I believe to be a major slump in the manufacturing industry, and it has caused us to slide into a major crisis. I am sure it has contributed to the very serious trade deficit we recorded in 1975 of some $8 billion in the so-called higher technology manufacturing field. That was $1 billion worse than it was the year before.
What does this mean? It means a loss of jobs, a loss of economic activity, and a loss of opportunities for present and future generations of Canadians.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
When we look at the flour industry and see what has happened to it on a global basis, and then when we examine what has happened to Canada relative to that world position, it is a very revealing exercise. World demand for flour has expanded from 65 million cwt. in 1954 to 95 million cwt. in 1974, an increase of 50 per cent. During this time Canada's share of this trade declined from 31 per cent to 11 per cent. In 1954 Canadian millers were exporting some 20 million cwt. annually. In 1975 our exports dropped more than 50 per cent, to some 8.5 million cwt.
In this connection the Minister of Agriculture indicated that the flour milling industry was a dying enterprise and that there was no hope of ever recovering it. Well, as far as the Minister of Agriculture's comments on the matter are concerned, I can only say that he is simply not looking at the potential which is available. For his information it was only Canada and Australia which experienced substantial declines in the export of flour. As far as the United States is concerned, its share has not fallen appreciably from its 1954 level. As a matter of fact its share has increased.
The European Common Market-and this is where there is a great deal of subsidy and a great deal of support for this industry-has expanded its exports from 15 million cwt. in 1954 to 64 million cwt. in 1974. Therefore to suggest that world export demand has fallen is simply sheer nonsense.
The actions which the government proposes to take as far as the removal of this particular subsidy is concerned would have the effect of increasing the freight costs to Canadian millers by 212 per cent. This cost has to be added to the cost of flour which is exported, and therefore it will have a very disastrous effect upon this very important secondary manufacturing industry.
As I said earlier, hon. members opposite have constantly suggested that we on this side of the House have had nothing to propose in the way of positive suggestions or positive alternatives.

speechtext:
In the past few weeks there has been disclosure of questionable transactions by some of our Crown corporations, and there has been the report of the Auditor General. These are items of a very serious nature which reflect upon the capacity, integrity, and competence of the government. The allegations regarding our Crown corporations have affected our reputation financially and politically-and now commercially-in the international field.
It is very disturbing to note that parliament and the government have lost control of the public purse. Our financial management and control mechanisms are grossly inadequate, weak and ineffective. Those systems at present are significantly below acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness.
What we are really saying is that Canadians can no longer rely on the government to act as a worthy trustee of tax dollars, because its waste, extravagance, frauds, use of excessive office space, haphazard manner of administering operations, overstating its accounts and the assets of Canada, flout-
December 6, 1976

ing of laws and guidelines, and its manner of contravening the provisions of the Financial Administration Act are part and parcel of a performance which is a sad commentary on its actions. It is therefore ironic that at this time of our history we should be asked to pass a bill calling for government restraint.
Frankly, so far as I am concerned, before the government can expect the co-operation of the people of Canada on restraint, it must by clear example show that it itself means to exercise restraint. In other words it must show by example that it has control of the public purse and that it is ever watchfully and prudently spending the public funds of Canadians. It must practice what it preaches. Not only must mechanics of accounting devices be put in place; ministers and other representatives of the government must show that they too are practising restraint. Frankly, the government so far has not demonstrated willingness to restrain spending-nor have the ministers demonstrated it by their actions.
The Liberal government has deliberately foisted two myths on the people of Canada, myths I shall seek to expose this evening. One is that it alone can keep Canada together, that it alone has the leadership qualities and the inspiration to keep the country together as a viable, united unit.
