subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note that since this bill was introduced on November 1, it has been considered on no less than 14 days and, according to my tabulation, so far 80 speakers have participated in the debate. On November 25 my colleague, the hon. member for Lamb-ton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) moved an amendment to defer second reading for six months. That might seem like an undue delay of the government's legislative program-if it had one.
I refer hon. members to the record of the present session of the Thirtieth Parliament of Canada. The number of bills introduced to date is 26; as far as I am aware only one, the act to provide for the resumption of port operations in Halifax, has passed all stages. A number of bills are presently under consideration, some of them in committee. But the government has no obvious plan, no legislative direction or goal toward which it is leading the country. As one columnist was moved to write recently:
This past summer, the government took three months to prepare its fall legislative program. What has it introduced? One major new item-a revised Immigration Act. Some budget bills left over from last June. Human rights legislation left over from the last session. An amendment to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. An amendment to the Canada Land Surveys Act. A bill to repeal the Satisfied Securities Act. A bill to eliminate double taxation between Canada and a few other countries. An amendment to the Historic Sites and Monuments Act.
What a list of housekeeping bills that is! But it certainly does not add up to a program which any government knowing the direction in which it was going would present to the House.
When I made an earlier contribution to the debate I referred to the restraint which could be exercised in the area of Crown corporations. There are some 43 Crown corporations listed in the table of contents of volume III of the Public

December 6, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures Accounts. I directed my remarks mainly to three of these, including Air Canada, which on a billion dollars of assets manages to come up with a loss of $3 million-not a big loss when compared with others in the operation of this country. Another I looked at was the CBC which on assets of $300 million manages to roll up a loss these days of over $300 million. I suppose there is even more opportunity in the area of the CNR, which on assets of $5 billion manages to turn a loss of $168 million.
I also mentioned the Post Office Department. This department has untold assets. We do not know how much they are and it is doubtful whether anyone does since all the real estate occupied by the Post Office is hidden away in the accounts of another department, the Department of Public Works. But the revenue of the Post Office amounted to $618 million and they managed to run a loss of 50 cents for every dollar they received for a total loss of $321 million.
I felt there was good potential for the government to get some restraint out of the corporations I mentioned. Since then, I have managed to look at more of these Crown corporations. It is difficult even to find out how many there are. The Auditor General has had an opportunity to say a few things about those corporations, too. As far as numbers are concerned, I referred a few moments ago to volume III of the Public Accounts of 1976 which lists 43 Crown corporations from Air Canada to Uranium Canada Limited. When I then turned to the Canada Year Book and found there were three different classes of these corporations, departmental corporations, agency corporations, and proprietary corporations, the matter became somewhat complicated. These institutions are specified in schedules B, C and D respectively of the Financial Administration Act. In any event, when I added them up in the Canada Year Book on government organization I only got 49, which is six more. The reason I said "only 49" is that when I went to the Auditor General's report I found that on pages 289 to 292 there are four tables of government-owned and controlled corporations and the total number there seems to be 73.
It is not surprising that the Public Accounts would not reflect all of them because one whole page of the appendix on page 292 of the Auditor General's Report lists 16 other corporations and not one of them is audited by the Auditor General. Furthermore, the footnote tells us that the financial statements of those corporations are not included in the Public Accounts and the notation is made: Reason not stated.
In addition to those 16 which are not included in the Public Accounts we find a further ten of various kinds which are not audited by the Auditor General, including some of the better known ones like Air Canada, CMHC, Petro-Canada and Polysar Limited. I shall not read them all but a fair number of them are also, for one reason or another, not included in the Public Accounts, even corporations like TELESAT and the Newfoundland and Labrador Development Corporation Limited. There are a further ten or so. Thus there are 26 which are not included in the Public Accounts, for what reason I cannot be certain.
Let me carry on briefly about what the Auditor General tells us-this is just a matter of numbers at the moment. Starting at page 303, the appendix to the reports on Crown corporations, he lists 23 Crown corporations with regard to which he made extensive recommendations, or perhaps one might call them criticisms. There is a footnote on that page indicating that the review of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Canada Salt Fish Corporation did not indicate any serious weakness. Presumably the remark is restricted to those two. The corollary is that the accounts of over 21 of the institutions listed on this page did reveal significant weaknesses, and I suggest this is the reason the next 140 pages of the Auditor General's report are taken up with observations and recommendations with regard to the faults and problems which were found in the accounts of those 21 Crown corporations.
We might easily ask ourselves why such a lot of fault-finding found its place in that report on these Crown corporations. I believe the Auditor General anticipated we might ask that question and I would refer now to the Conspectus of the report. On page two, the Auditor General reminds us that last year he had reported that-
The present state of the financial management and control systems of the departments and agencies of the Government of Canada is significantly below acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness.
We all hoped last year in the committee that the government would do something about these recommendations which had been made. But in his summary of the report this year the Auditor General notes that his study led to the following observations with regard to the Crown corporations which had been reviewed. I should like to read six of them here. This is on pages two and three of the Conspectus.
1.	No central government agency recognizes the need to identify all the corporations owned or controlled by the Government of Canada.
Is it any wonder that the numbers are different in all these publications? No central agency has been asked to undertake this task. Of course this is the basis of one of the prime recommendations which the Auditor General made.
2.	Commercial enterprises in the private sector are subject to a greater degree of financial accountability than Crown corporations.
We receive hundreds, if not thousands of complaints from businessmen who are trying to do business in Canada and contributing through their taxes to the well being of the country. How can the government ask these people to co-operate and carry on their businesses in a proper manner when the government's own businesses, which in some cases are competing with them, and using the taxpayers dollars to do so, are not subject to as stringent a degree of financial accountability as are corporations in the private sector?
Thirdly, the Auditor General says this:
Financial management and control is not a priority within Crown corporations.
It is often said, Mr. Speaker, that the private sector has profits to measure its efficiency but that government corporations have to rely on a different measure of their efficiency,

December 6, 1976

one measure of course being financial management and control. However, after great study the Auditor General has stated that financial management and control are not a priority item with this government. There can be no other method of measuring the effectiveness, or lack thereof, of government corporations than some such system as this.
The fourth item, if I may again quote the Auditor General, is this:
The annual deficits and net debt of the Government of Canada are substantially understated due to the manner of accounting for Crown corporations.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, if there are 22 of them that are not included in the public accounts-and probably they have made great losses as well-it is obvious to anyone reading the financial picture that he does not have the total financial picture and is not able to say what are the actual results of the operations of the Government of Canada. When we have a situation where the stewards of the assets of the country are unwilling or unable, one or the other, to give a report to the owners, then the time has come for us to make some very drastic changes.
The fifth point that the Auditor General makes is this:
Parliament is presented with incomplete and fragmented financial plans and inadequate financial reports.
In the four years I have been here 1 have been hearing about the inadequacy of our examination of the estimates, the inadequacy of committees, the inadequacy of information given to members of parliament duly elected by the people of Canada to oversee their affairs. If we cannot get the information from the government, then the people of Canada are in a much worse state than they think they are.
The sixth and final observation in the Auditor General's study is this:
Financing practices would preclude evaluating management performance even if central agencies had the responsibility to do so.
That is telling us a couple of very important things, Mr. Speaker. First of all it is telling us that the central agencies do not really have responsibility for evaluating management performance. Secondly, it is telling us that even if the central agencies did have responsibility for evaluating management performance, the practices that are employed would preclude any evaluation being made.
The conclusion the Auditor General comes to this year, after that condemnation in his 1975 report, is this, and I suggest it is a very important if not major conclusion:
In the majority of the Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control is weak and ineffective. Moreover, co-ordination and guidance by central government agencies of financial management and control practices in these Crown corporations are virtually non-existent.
The government has published book after book of estimates, votes, public accounts, statements by Crown corporations, annual reports and so on, yet the Auditor General concludes that financial management and control practices are virtually non-existent. I do not know how Canadians or the members of this parliament can expect to have the government achieve any kind of restraint when the government has no way of knowing
Restraint of Government Expenditures what amounts it is spending and whether it is even spending the money to the best advantage.
I should like to make a last reference to the Auditor General's latest report. He poses to us this question: what caused this alarming state of affairs to develop? And secondly: what can and should be done to rectify it? After all, Mr. Speaker, we have to know the answers to these questions when we try to account to our electors who sent us here to take care of their affairs. The Auditor General finds that he is not exactly able to pin down the cause of the state of affairs developing, and admits it is partly conjecture, but he goes on to say in reply to the second question:
However, it seems clear that the present unsatisfactory and vulnerable situation came about because certain key recommendations on financial management and control made by the Royal Commission on Government Organization (Glassco Commission) in 1962 were not implemented.
Again, Mr. Speaker, in the four years I have been here I have been trying to find out from the government when these recommendations, which were acceptable in principle and in large part in detail in the report of 1962, would be implemented, but I have not been given the answer. If the government is seriously concerned about restraint, it is time it gave us those answers.
The Auditor General goes on to state that there are other factors contributing to this situation and gives a few of them. The first is:
An attitude (tempered to some extent during periods of constraint such as at present) on the part of many managers at all levels that funds are readily available and that they themselves are not personally accountable for ensuring that public funds and assets placed at their disposal are under strict control at all times and that funds are expended prudently, economically, and with the utmost concern that good value is received for money spent.
If we do not have managers who are capable or willing to expend money prudently and economically and with concern for value received, then I suggest that any bill that the government puts before the House to encourage restraint on the part of government is a useless exercise, to say the least.
The second factor that appears to have contributed to the inadequate financial controls that now exist, says the Auditor General, is this:
A genuine and widespread lack of comprehension on the part of senior officials of government as to what effective management and control of public funds actually consists of.
So having said that managers are not doing their jobs, for whatever reason, Mr. Speaker, he now says that to a large extent the managers do not comprehend what it is that effective management and control consists of. If they do not know what they are supposed to be doing, Mr. Speaker, how can the government expect them to exercise any measure of restraint?
The third factor put forward by the Auditor General is this:
A lack of recognition by these same senior officials of the role a senior departmental financial officer could and should play in assisting them to administer with prudence, probity and economy the public funds for which they are accountable and thereby manage more effectively the organizations over which they have jurisdiction.
Having already said that managers do not have the right attitude, and then having said that they did not comprehend

December 6, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
what it was they were supposed to do, the Auditor General now says that even if they did comprehend, they could not recognize what it was that the financial officers should be doing for them in order to make their job easier.
The fourth and last point is the unawareness among deputy heads of the characteristic of a qualified, competent and experienced senior financial officer and the contribution such a person could make as a member of the organization's top executive team, given properly defined responsibilities and adequate authority and resources. What that tells us is that there has been some restraint in the wrong areas. In other words, the managers do not have available to them qualified, competent and experienced senior financial officers who can take charge of the expenditures and accounting in the various Crown corporations.
I have dealt at some length with the Auditor General's report and Crown corporations. I think it is important because these Crown corporations tend to be brushed aside. Time after time when questions are asked in the House about them, the ministers are given to pass over the answers and say that Crown corporations have nothing to do with them, that they are independent bodies. Well, the government may find that a convenient answer to give in the House, but the taxpayer knows that it is his money that is being spent in those Crown corporations, so he wants value for it.
I think we could argue in another debate whether these 73, or whatever the number is, Crown corporations are necessary, or whether in fact many of them are necessary. I have made that point a number of times and I think it is obvious there are degrees of endeavour in which the government must be involved, such as national defence. There is also the other extreme-degrees of activity in which the government should certainly not be involved, such as hotels operated by the CNR. In between I suggest there are many questionable areas where the government, if it is serious about restraint, could relieve at lot of investment pressure on government budgets as well as reduce enormously the annual operating losses in those corporations.
I would like to make some other observations about some government programs, which the government considers so good, by referring to what was written about them in some newpapers recently. I will do so lest members opposite think I am making all this up, that it is an opinion singular unto myself. These items point to anything but an attitude of restraint on the part of the government.
The first is an article in the Globe and Mail which appeared within the last two weeks. It refers to the purchase and modification of a fishing vessel which was to be given or loaned to the Republic of Columbia by the Canadian government, to be used in a project for technical assistance in fisheries training methods. The government bought this ship for $175,000. Before it was finished, it had a total investment in that ship of $828,000. A month after that, in April of this year, Columbia refused to accept the ship because it was

unstable and unsuitable for the proposed operations. The government has not quite decided yet what alternative course of action to take to dispose of this ship for $828,000.
A little while before that, in April of 1974-and this is another matter which has not been resolved yet-the Department of the Environment acquired a leasehold interest in some property in the greater Vancouver area for the Pacific Environment Centre. The department paid $4 million to the previous tenant and then agreed to lease back about 20 per cent of it, 91/2 acres, for a renewable ten year term at an annual rental of $ 1 for the first ten years. The present worth of that lease is observed to be $702,000.
The next could be considered humorous had it not caused the loss of $13,000. Somebody in the Customs and Excise branch made a mistake. Instead of drawing a cheque for 370 Dutch florins, they requisitioned a cheque for 370,000 Dutch florins. When that was converted to a Bank of Canada draft, the cost of the draft was $157,000. We will have to give somebody credit because they did not mail out that draft for $157,000. Somebody found the error, but by the time it was found and they got the draft back into the bank, and made out a new draft for 370 Dutch florins, the exchange rate had turned unfavourable and they had to sustain a loss of $13,000 caused by the decline in that exchange rate.
It is not only in Crown corporations or even only in the accounting for government business that the government has problems which make its restraint program look somewhat foolish. Another program which I should like to draw to the attention of the House is the government housing program. We keep hearing from the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and his predecessor-and perhaps even from several ministers in the past few years because we have had a number of housing ministers-about the housing shortage in Canada and how they will get the housing starts up to 250,000, and so on. There may have been a housing shortage a while ago and there are certainly people in Canada who have a hard time finding housing, but in no way can it be argued that there is a housing shortage in Canada today. It is easy to find all over Canada today in rental accommodation with vacancy rates of 20 per cent. How can there be a housing shortage if 20 per cent of apartments in certain areas are empty?
At the same time, in all but the government assisted programs where people are buying AHOP houses, for example in all but the lowest price single family units, there is a tremendous stock of unsold houses. These are not the very expensive houses but the ones in larger cities probably, although not always, in the price range of, say, $80,000. People these days just cannot afford to get into those houses. For the government to say that there is a housing shortage is to draw a red herring across the trail. It can be shown statistically that there is lots of housing available. It is not a housing problem but a money problem. The government might consider that it is more costly to be honest about it and put the money where the problem is, but in the meantime it keeps offering these programs and spending money at a time when it says it is trying to restrain spending. The government spends money on programs to
December 6, 1976

provide housing, which causes the private sector to be stuck with a huge inventory.
I have predicted this before and I will say again that I do not think we will go through this winter without some major financial failures-bankruptcies, if you want to call them that-in the private sector, because the private sector has been hampered at every turn by government at one level or another in its efforts to provide housing for Canadians. I suppose that a few examples will be in order because people will say, "What is the government doing, it is helping these builders?"
It did not help the housing situation when the federal government removed its incentive to rental housing in 1971. All that did was remove a lot of rental housing from the market, and it probably precipitated the tightest housing shortage for apartments that we had seen in the years right up to now in the larger centres. After all, interest rates are an effect of federal government policies, and the government seems to be unable to take any steps to make it easier for Canadians to buy houses in the way of getting them lower interest rates. Interest is probably the major cost in making up the housing component.
The federal government is not the only one responsible; provincial governments can take steps and have taken steps to make things difficult for the housing industry, such as putting land freezes around certain city areas, which automatically drive up prices and make it more difficult for Canadians to buy houses. Then, of course, civic governments also make it difficult and cause tremendous delays which result in higher costs by way of carrying charges and so forth for the land upon which housing can be built.
The federal government can get the restraint program on stream by cutting out some of the programs it thinks are important but which the industry does not. Then industry could be allowed to get down to work, and we would not have the situation we now have of Canadian builders and investors being forced to take their money to other countries which are more attractive from an investment point of view, and using Canadian money to provide housing for Americans or nationals of other countries.
Lest anyone thinks that the housing industry itself is crying for this government's aid, I would like to refer to a recent article in the Globe and Mail which arose out of an interview with industry leaders in the real estate field. They say that they are concerned about the business climate and the ways in which governments can and do intervene to the consternation of property owners at large. They are also worried that Canada might import programs from other countries, because they say the government seems to like importing ideas. They give this example:
In recent years, real estate people and real estate boards have had to deal with anti-development and anti-business municipal councils wanting to change the ground rules for the use of property, and seeming to disparage the very idea of private property ownership.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
They have seen provincial governments freezing development rights in the name of planning. They have seen rent control slow the market by making people who could afford to move ... too comfortable in their present quarters.
This is probably one of their strongest condemnations:
They have seen the federal Government copy U.S. authorities in applying anti-combines laws in the consumer field, requiring a four-year effort by the Canadian Real Estate Association to persuade Ottawa that the Multiple Listing Service is a real service and not a conspiracy.
That is four years of unproductive work on the part of an industry just to prove to this government that what it was doing was not so bad after all.
I see that my time is running out, and I would like to touch on just one or two other aspects of the government's restraint program.
I liked very much the observation of another editorial in the Globe and Mail about business, tax revenue, the intervention, shall we say, of the government into various fields of endeavour and so forth. The summary comment, if I could call it that, is this: "Wealth can't be redistributed until it has been created". We know that the government has a great interest in redistributing wealth. Many of the ministers have made statements that they are concerned about income redistribution, but if they do not let entrepreneurs in small businesses and big corporations-those people who produce wealth-get to work and stop interfering, there will not be any wealth to redistribute. Canada would not be the first country which would find itself in that position.
There is another huge area which is just beginning to bubble on the burners of concern in Canada, and that has to do with indexed pensions. Obviously I am not going to be able to get into that tonight, but I should say that the Canadian Institute of Actuaries has studied the situation in connection with the unfunded indexed pensions of the Government of Canada for civil servants and others, and they claim that more adequate and appropriate information on the cost of providing these pensions is needed in order to answer widespread concerns about financing the program. They refer to the Treasury Board report as follows:
... "the speciousness or the dubious validity of so many of the statements made and arguments advanced have aroused the suspicion or outright condemnation of practically every professional actuary who has examined the document."
They say that no attempt has been made to recognize the currently accruing cost, nor is there any requirement that the actuarial experience be subject to periodic actuarial review. There is a huge area for restraint that the government owes it to the Canadian taxpayer to have a look at.
Just before I sit down I would like to ask a question of the government. How can we have restraint of any kind under any kind of a proposal when we have no systems, no accountability, and no concern for the amount of money which is spent, and when we do not even know on what we are spending the money?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in previous weeks much has been said about the merits and the inadequacies of Bill C-19, and the debate has been lengthy. While I do not intend to reiterate the arguments our party has

Restraint of Government Expenditures
presented, I will make brief mention of clause 15. It is with pleasure that I learned that the government has decided to concede to opposition demands and withdraw-for the moment, anyway-this portion of the bill.
As my colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), and others have pointed out, the major reasons for establishing the "at and east" rates in 1961 are still valid today. It is emphasized that these freight rates were designed to encourage the continued use of eastern ports to help keep Canadian flour companies competitive in world markets, to promote and assist development and expansion of Canada's grain industry, and to benefit the Canadian economy by providing mill, transportation, and port employment, as well as helping Canada's balance of trade position.
I might add that in 1976 the maintenance of these freight rates is most important. The western farm economy saw a bumper crop of wheat this year, and it is going to be an essential part of the government's plan to market this wheat. It seems to me that in this instance these freight rate subsidies will be very important in moving at least some of the western wheat through the eastern ports and through the flour mills which still exist in Canada. I can see this as a benefit to western farmers as well as eastern Canadians, and I think it is entirely a good move to remove this clause.
One thing which has struck many of us in reading and listening to the debate on this bill is the sharp contrast between the waste and inefficiencies revealed in the Auditor General's report and the government's paltry attempts to restrain spending, as outlined in Bill C-19. It is difficult for my constituents to understand the logic of reducing family allowance payments-they would have been increased if this bill had not come forward-when the Auditor General's report reveals gross mismanagement of public funds on the part of this government.
Perhaps the size of the bureaucracy is one of the factors which has led to the following situation. Instead of relying on its own marketing branch, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited paid $15 million to Eisenberg to sell CANDU reactors to South Korea. Not only does the sale raise serious moral questions in view of its implications for nuclear proliferation, but in carrying out the transaction the Auditor General claims that $8 million of the Canadian taxpayers' money was not adequately accounted for. AECL made a payment of $2.5 million to another agent in a deal to Argentina, a deal which will ultimately cost Canadian taxpayers as much as $100 million. AECL was criticized by the Auditor General for failing to report these pending losses.
It has cost Canadian taxpayers nearly $950,000 a year for a Vancouver property rented by the Department of the Environment which signed no lease and presently has no use for the property. The land was to be used for the Pacific Environment Centre but it is lying vacant due to budgetary restraints. In the same deal $4 million was paid to the previous tenant for 9.5

acres of land for which the government now admits it has no use.
A fishing vessel was outfitted for $828,000 and then it was found to be unseaworthy.
A shipment of $64,000 worth of potatoes was sent to Haiti in December and when they arrived it was discovered that frost and seawater had destroyed them.
I should like to comment on the government's appointment of a royal commission to study these problems. As the Auditor General revealed in his report, there is a great deal of mismanagement of funds, and he made various suggestions for solving some of the problems. Instead, the government has used the tactic of appointing a royal commission to study the situation and to report within a year or a year and a half. This is seen as a stalling tactic- perhaps the whole thing will die after a year and the public outcry will not be as great.
One of the main reasons I rose tonight was to speak on clause 14 of the bill, which provides for an amendment to the Western Grain Stabilization Act. If enacted this will mean that while farmers continue to pay into the fund at the rate of a 2 per cent levy, the federal government will be able to doctor the fund's account, writing in the amount to be paid but in fact withholding the actual payment until a later date when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) deems it advisable to make the outlay. Surely such accounting practices must be questioned.
I know a number of western farmers who are affected by the stabilization act and who are questioning this procedure. During the debate on that bill I remember that this party offered a number of suggestions on how to cut the costs of administration of the act and keep them to a minimum. It was suggested that the crop insurance staff could act as the inspectors rather than hiring a great many additional employees for Statistics Canada to go around and gather the information. It was also proposed that we have individual accounts rather than the aggregate account. This would assure each farmer of protection in his own situation during each year rather than having an aggregate payment when the total prairie economy was in a deficit position.
A recent edition of the Financial Post had an article which claimed that the price of wheat is dropping-in fact the price of all grains has dropped this year- and that costs are still rising, and that if we take a five-year average there may well be a payout in the coming year. The article claimed that a shift in production costs could aggravate the size of the payout, and that Statistics Canada estimates the 1976 costs are 10 per cent above 1975 levels. The writer blamed the opposition critics for not passing the original grain stabilization bill in 1971. He said that the five year average would then have been front loaded with low return years. Instead, the Liberal government can expect to have yet another albatross hanging from its neck when it goes to the polls in 1978, according to this article. I think the opposition can take that kind of criticism when we are getting extra income for prairie farmers. The suggestions we put forward were ignored in the
December 6, 1976

debate on the grain stabilization act and now we find the government trying to cut corners.
A recent study of what has happened to prairie grain prices and prairies farm incomes shows that the situation is not too good. The price of every farm product, other than rapeseed, has declined during the past year. The cattle industry has endured its second year of depressed prices the world over, and it is the same for hogs. Hog prices ranged from $68.22 a cwt. to $68.72 last year, and this year hogs are trading for $20 less, with prices averaging $47.35. Major grains have suffered the same fate. A comparison of cash prices with last year's prices shows that feed wheat No. 3 red spring traded for $2.76 a bushel, when last year it traded at $3.82; oats No. 2 Canadian western traded for $1.18 and last year it traded for $1.64 per bushel; barley is selling for $1.87 for No. 1 feed when last year's price was $2.36.
The only commodity I could find that has remained stable or gone up slightly is rapeseed. Yet this article claims that prices are going up, while economists in the Alberta department of agriculture anticipate a 5 per cent increase compared to 13 per cent a year ago and 18 per cent the year previous in the costs of production. As these costs rise and prices decrease, farmers will look to the act passed by parliament for help. With the worsening financial position of our farmers, stabilization payments may well be essential for their economic survival. This applies particularly to small farmers.
If the present amendment to the stabilization act is adopted, the government may be forced to scramble for funds in order to meet its commitments to farmers. I believe the farmers' levy is paid into the consolidated revenue fund. The government has stated that if it has to put up money which would normally be part of its revenue it will just write that amount off. The same is true of interest payments. If the government is called on to make such contributions under the stabilization plan, will it be able to keep its promises to farmers if it is suddenly confronted with large demands, the fund may be asked to pay out?
That concludes the comments I wish to make on this bill before it goes to committee. I think it is important to note that the government's planned withdrawal of the clause to do with the "at and east" rates represents a victory for the Conservative party.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the principle point of objection which I raised earlier and which other hon. members raised will be dealt with, if it has not already been dealt with; therefore I do not intend to take much of the time of the House in making my point. I have expressed it four times this spring and summer, together with the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). Others have joined us in speaking two or three times on the same theme in the present debate. This is my second contribution; I hope the House will forgive me for it.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
To me the issues involved were rather important; they affected the ports of Halifax and Saint John to a somewhat different degree than they affected most other ports of Canada. Allow me to make a general point to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang); I am sure he has heard from others what I am about to say and he will not be surprised by my comments; then, let me make two specific points in addition, and I will cease and desist.
My general point concerns the minister's argument as set forth, beginning on page 956 of Hansard of November 10. I think that philosophy is a good philosophy to apply. It is good to say that transport should bear its proper share of costs in Canada. I say it is a good philosophy if that approach is used all over Canada, that is to say, if it is used in connection with the Crownest Pass rates, the Welland Canal, the St. Lawrence River rates, as well as the special deal which Halifax and Saint John enjoy by virtue of section 272 of the Railway Act.
I think one could possibly expect the public of Canada in time to accept the argument that we must change our system with regard to transport costs, so that the person in Vancouver will not feel that he has been given a worse deal than, say, the person in Trois-Rivieres. To me it is as simple as that. While such changes might gore a lot of people, at least the Canadian people could stomach them, provided they apply across the board. But once you single out one part of Canada and make such changes in one part, you get yourself into the sort of difficulty the minister has encountered. I say that in order to make my general point.
May I now deal with the two specific points which the minister himself set forth in his speech, as indicated on page 957 of Hansard. If the matter were to continue without correction, I am sure I could speak for 40 minutes and ask for more time to finish these wise remarks in future; but I will not do it because I understand that the issue will be dealt with. Perhaps I should thank the hon. member for Vegreville, who joined me in making the initial comment on the matter. I thank the hon. members who have dealt with it more than once since it was raised initially. Having patted myself on the back and not heard resounding cheers from other parts of the House, I will simply have to let the record speak for itself. Let the record determine if we were able to accomplish what we set out to do.
Having said all this, I make the following two points sincerely to the minister. I have read his remarks about the milling industry with care. He talked about a $9 million a year subsidy to the milling industry; however, I understand that the subsidy to the industry was no more than $3 million a year. The people to whom I talked do not know where the figure $9 million came from; nor do I know its origin. Be that as it may, the milling industry would like the minister to initiate a long-range program, or at least they would like to see a few years ahead. Because the offending clause will be withdrawn in committee, I believe, there will be an opportunity either for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) or the Minister of Transport to say what long-range help, if any, it is planned to give the milling industry. That is my first point.

December 6, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
My second point concerns the unit train concept. Exactly what is the government planning in this regard? The minister considered that the unit train concept would partly answer our difficulties; he thinks that it will provide Saint John and Halifax with the answer which is not now available. I point out that the minister neglected to say originally that 30 per cent of the grain moves into those two ports by boat. Perhaps he lost sight of that fact. This matter should also be explored in committee before a new program is presented. I understand that the unit train concept was first raised several months ago, when the hon. member for Vegreville and I first raised it as a question. I notice that as a result of our speeches there were discussions involving the National Harbours Board, the Canadian Wheat Board, Canadian National Railways, as well as at least one department of the provincial government of Nova Scotia which was involved in those discussions. I will not belabour the point, since I do not wish to make a long speech.
Discussion of the unit train concept started back in April, or perhaps May. In the present debate the minister trotted out his most recent arguments concerning the unit train on November 10 when he made his speech in the House. What happened between April or May and November to the concept of the unit train? How much serious study was carried out in that regard? Were the road beds examined? Were the economics of the proposal examined? Did anyone consider that you would need at least one large elevator system either in Saskatchewan or Manitoba to feed the unit train? Although the people of Nova Scotia are not from Missouri, they at least would want to know more about this bold concept. I know that when I was raising this matter initially in the House, I was beaten down by the large headlines in the Chronicle Herald and Mail Star. When the unit train concept was first proposed I was lucky to find my comments reported a little bit above the obituary column. The fact is that political obituaries have now put an end to clause 15 of Bill C-19, which does not hurt me one single bit. But we have not seen any headlines in the Chronicle Herald and the Mail Star to the effect that the unit train concept is going on. If something could be said about getting one's head above the obituaries and getting one's head above the Minister of Transport, I think there could be possibilities in that glittering idea, but with all respect to the hon. gentleman he has to bring more facts and figures to the House.
I said I would be brief, Mr. Speaker, and I intend to keep that promise. I am pleased that somebody over there on that side has seen the wisdom of our fight against clause 15. A number of members opposite may not be very happy to know that it is to be withdrawn. But at least it is done. The people of Saint John and Halifax have to thank the members of parliament who carried on this fight and made this victory possible, and on their part, through you, Mr. Speaker, I thank those members now. I will also say a kind word for the ministry which succumbed to the inevitable, because if this had not been done it would have been either closure or Christmas. It would not have been both.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not had an opportunity to speak on Bill C-19 and I certainly appreciate being able to offer a few remarks on the general question of restraint.
Speaking very generally, I think I should say first of all that the bill is wrongly named. The government calls it a restraint bill. If we look at its title, we find it says "An Act to Amend or Repeal Certain Statutes to Enable Restraint of Government Expenditures". Mr. Speaker, the fact is that the government does not need a bill in the form we have before us in order to bring about more restraint in its spending programs. It could have done that last year, two years ago, or five years ago. There can be no doubt that the government has been the most unrestrained, as far as spending is concerned, of any in our history.
Let us not forget, as we come to the conclusion of this debate on Bill C-19, that when the present administration was elected in the fiscal year 1968, the budget amounted in total to $9,927 million. Within six years it had succeeded in more than doubling expenditure at the federal level. To put the picture in another way, it took over one hundred years of confederation to reach a budget of somewhat under $10 billion, and within six further years government spending had brought the nation to the level of a budget of $20,473 million. Within the last three years the government doubled that figure again, so we now have a budget of $42,250 million. Yet the administration has the gall to expect credit for keeping expenditure at that level, one which I am pointing out is four times the spending level experienced in the fiscal year 1968.
In the last three years the government has caused federal spending to rise at the rate of 35 per cent per year. In the current year how often have we heard the claim that while spending last year rose by 18 per cent, this year it will only rise by 14 per cent? We have heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) say on several occasions that it is intended to keep federal spending in line with the growth of the gross national product. That is not the case. The government has already broken its own guidelines. Present indications are that the gross national product in this country will be up by approximately 11 per cent this year, yet the government on its own admission will increase its spending by 14 per cent, 3 per cent higher than the growth of the GNP. To their credit, the provinces have been more restrained. They have collectively kept their spending to the 11 per cent level, which is approximately the growth we shall experience in the current year. The reason I dwell on this is because I believe it is a misnomer for the government to be pretending that Bill C-19 is somehow its restraint program in action.
What is the effect of this tremendous increase in government spending at the federal level? I should like to refer hon. members, first of all, to the November 15, 1976, report on the Canadian economy, "Economy Outlook," put out by Oppen-heimer and Co. of New York. This report was written by Martin Pomp, and I would stress that contrary to what the government is trying to insinuate, namely, that the sell-off of our dollar was somehow the result of the popular verdict in the

December 6, 1976

Quebec election, this report was written on November 15, the very date of that election. This is what the report states:
Based on our analysis of U.S-Canadian relative inflation and costs, we believe the Canadian dollar is worth between U.S. $0.86 and $0.92, significantly below the current rate of $1.02. While our confidence in the timing is not great, we believe the Canadian dollar will slide from current levels in the current year.
That was written on November 15 and we now know that the dollar has declined by approximately 5 per cent in the last few weeks. But what I find most interesting is the analysis contained in this report-the reason why the Canadian dollar has been slipping. For example, we find this statement:
Our analysis shows that Canada faces some pressing problems that are not generally appreciated in this country: too rapidly rising government sector spending and large public sector deficits;
What could be more clear? Our affairs have been in the hands of a big spending government which has caused the country to live beyond its means, and we are now paying the penalty through a falling dollar in relation to the American dollar.
Let me read further from this summary which Oppenheimer and Co. put out.
Looking at the wholesale price index (all commodities) on the 1967 base- chosen because it was a year of equilibrium in U.S.-Canada trade-Canada's inflation through the second quarter of 1976 has been 7 per cent greater than that of the U.S., but the currency is now 11 per cent higher than the 1967 average; thus, the Canadian dollar can be said to be "worth" U.S. $0.87.
Again, what could be more clear? The government has brought about inflation which in turn has resulted in our dollar being worth about 15 per cent less than it was trading at a short while ago, according to this American analysis. I quote further:
Canadian unit labour costs (manufacturing) have risen in U.S. dollar terms 5 per cent more than have U.S. costs since 1967, so that an $0.88 exchange rate can be said to be appropriate on this measure of relative inflation. Canada's unit labour costs have risen 15 per cent more than U.S. unit costs since 1971, and are a harbinger of suppressed inflation within the current WPI and CPI figures under Canadian price and wage controls.
Then the second item in the Oppenheimer report is this:
-Canadian manufacturing is very much non-competitive; manufacturing unemployment has risen faster than that of the over-all economy, and manufacturing has declined from 23.0 per cent to 21.4 per cent of gross domestic product since 1971. Canada's share of world trade in manufactures has fallen by 22 per cent over the last eight years, and by 28 per cent if one excludes automotive exports-
The first point I want to make is that since this government took office in 1968 it has caused excessive federal government spending, and in no way is the government doing much more than mere window dressing in the introduction of Bill C-19, which is now before us. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker-my colleague from Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) has already referred to this this evening-when the Minister of Finance introduced his May 25 budget he stated he was going to try to keep spending within a limit of $42,250 million. At that time we stated there was at least $1,025 million which we could identify that could be reduced in the spending estimates if we had the opportunity to do so.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
Those savings included $125 million in the Post Office. I would certainly like to hear the new Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) tell us why he cannot save at least $125 million in the spending estimates of the Post Office. Secondly, we felt $250 million could have been saved through cutbacks in consulting contracts which the government has been so lavish in giving to many of its friends.

We also felt that $150 million could be saved by stabilizing the civil service. Based on the Auditor General's recommendations of last year-I emphasize last year, not this year-we felt there could have been $50 million saved in administrative expenses. Do I have to remind hon. members, Mr. Speaker, that we felt this saving could have been divided in this way? Some $475 million could have been given by way of incentives to the economy, especially in the form of a personal income tax break in order to get the economy rolling.

speechtext:
In addition to giving those tax breaks to the hard pressed Canadian taxpayer, we also thought $75 million could be given in the form of incentives for research and development in the private sector. What a contrast, Mr. Speaker, to what we find in Bill C-19, which proposes to discontinue the very act that was set up to encourage research

December 6, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures and development in the industrial sector; I refer, of course, to clause 10 of the bill.
Again, we advocated that there should be $75 million given to help export sales by way of incentives, especially to try to get our small businessman more competitive in world markets. We felt that medical research deserved another $25 million, and I only wish that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, instead of worrying about his rich friends, would have gone along with an extra $25 million for medical research.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, we felt small business should be given an export incentive and also a fee for the filing of federal forms. Collectively those two items would have accounted for $50 million of the $1,025 million that we could see could be eliminated from the spending estimates of the government. The remaining $550 million we proposed to use to reduce the deficit which the financiers of this country-the international financiers judging from our plunging dollar-would very much welcome.
That is our position, Mr. Speaker. We believe it is a more meaningful position as far as restraint is concerned. Above all it is a more meaningful position in order to get the economy of Canada running into higher gear, to bring about greater prosperity, and to give Canadians the jobs they deserve but which are being denied them by this government.
Just on that point, Mr. Speaker, it is very interesting to note an exchange that took place during "Question Period", not in this House but on CTV last Saturday. The air time was Sunday but the printed version I have was released on Saturday. Tony Westall was questioning the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) and was pointing out in a very effective way that the government has been totally inconsistent in that less than a year ago it was proposing to cancel various direct employment programs, such as Opportunities for Youth, a large part of the LIP program, and the Company of Young Canadians. Yet as Mr. Westall pointed out, just a year later the government was reinventing the very same programs. What did the Minister of Manpower and Immigration say in reply to that, Mr. Speaker? This is what he said:
Then to give you the other answer that I heard a judge give once, it would appear that it does not appear to appear to us now as it appears to have appeared to us then. It's been changed.
What an absolutely totally inept, indecisive government we have in Canada to make such a declaration!

subtopic: MANPOWER-SUGGESTED NEED FOR REVISION OF PUBLICATION "CANADIAN CLASSIFICATION AND DICTIONARY OF OCCUPATIONS"
MANPOWER-SUGGESTED NEED FOR REVISION OF PUBLICATION "CANADIAN CLASSIFICATION AND DICTIONARY OF OCCUPATIONS"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Human Rights Act which was introduced on November 29 prohibits discrimination in employment areas under federal jurisdiction on a number of grounds, including sex, race and national or ethnic origin. The bill, by its inclusion of the concept of equal pay for work of equal value, sets a framework within which equality of economic opportunities for women and minority groups can be achieved. However, that achievement is going to depend on a number of factors, not the least of which is the quality of job evaluation.
The "Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupations" prepared by the Department of Manpower in conjunction with Statistics Canada, which is generally regarded as the basis for job evaluation in the public service, Crown corporations, and other federal agencies, is very much better in many respects than its American counterpart, the "Dictionary of Occupational Titles." However, it has rigidities and limitations, particularly in dealing with the service occupations which I find generally underrated, and since service occupations are mainly staffed by women and immigrants, this underrating needs correction if the intent of the Human Rights Act is to be met.
As I pointed out in my speech of October 19, the "Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupations" is a usefull work for industrial type skills which are, first, easily measured; second, historically regarded as wage related; third, can be observed directly on the shop floor; and, fourth, can be measured or quantified in some way.
Personal service occupations, on the other hand, involve qualitative factors, for example, empathy or ability to encourage a child's intellectual and emotional development. I have every sympathy for those who find it difficult to quantify quality. However, I do think it urgent that ways be found to improve on the present method of measurement. The CCDO, for example, makes a distinction between supervising and instructing, with the latter being regarded as a more skilled function. Thus, a foster mother is considered to supervise children, while a dog trainer is considered to instruct dogs.
An occupation which sounds strangely old fashioned now- CCDO was published in 1971-entitled, "Instructor, Charm Course" indicates higher requirements in general education, specific vocational preparation, greater skill in dealing with data and people in order to teach "groups of women" such
December 6, 1976

things as "shaking hands, entering and leaving automobiles and turning around", than are required for a foster mother who is entrusted with the care of a small child.
The low rating for foster mother and child care attendant probably reflects male bias, inexperience, or both, with a woman's caring, nurturing qualities being seen as either proof of woman's greater spirituality, on which one cannot set a price, or alternatively, as a simple instinctual matter for which, of course, neither intelligence, education nor training is needed.
But perhaps another bias is that education and training must always happen in a classroom and after the age of seven, and there is a total blindness to the way small children learn by experience and to the qualities of heart and mind that are needed to create an optimum learning situation in a home.
Another bias that one might see here perhaps is the bias in favour of formal education. For example, a nursery school teacher with a university education seems to be graded quite appropriately, but there is a tremendous difference, and I think an inappropriate one, between that teacher and a nursery school aide.
Finally, the other bias that I see in this is a bias in favour of a specialist against a generalist. There is perhaps no realization that it may take as much ability to be generally competent in a number of spheres as to be extremely competent in one narrow area. So, as I have said before, while the CCDO is a great improvement on its American counterpart, and the difficulties in improving the personal service occupation descriptions are considerable, nevertheless I think this is an absolutely essential prerequisite for any sensible and realistic administration of the Human Rights Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. Arthur Portelance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: MANPOWER-SUGGESTED NEED FOR REVISION OF PUBLICATION "CANADIAN CLASSIFICATION AND DICTIONARY OF OCCUPATIONS"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the updating of occupations in the Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupations will lead to a review of the service worker group for April 1, 1978.
The reassessment of every classification in each group is a routine matter within the context of such a review. When the reassessment of the service trade group does start, we certainly shall consider the possibility of taking the "foster parent" group from the residual group under which it is currently classified into a new group, together with other occupations involved with child care.
Another aspect of the updating procedure involves the analysis of functions in any new occupation, as well as in all those currently appearing in the CCDO. Any change will include a review of descriptive factors such as general education, specific occupational training, physical activities, environment conditions and worker functions. Inclusion of the DPT numerical system to describe an occupation is based on the assumption that each worker has to deal with data, people and things. The first aim of this system is to supply a standardized terminology to sum up what a worker does. As any other standardized system, this one must from time to time include cases that do
Adjournment Debate
not exactly fit into a system. We must also keep in mind that descriptions do not state what should be, but what seems to exist at the time the occupational analysis was performed.
General education and specific occupational training levels for occupations such as "foster parent" are very difficult to determine, although a minimum of formal and informal education and experience certainly are a prerequisite, as is shown by the CCDO. A high level in both cases is no criterion of success in such work.
Just as the Canadian labour scene changes, so do we attempt to keep the Canadian classification up to date. We shall pay special attention to such and other similar factors.

subtopic: SEARCH AND RESCUE-REASON FOR DELAY IN RESCUING PASSENGERS FROM A DAMAGED TWIN OTTER IN THE ARCTIC
SEARCH AND RESCUE-REASON FOR DELAY IN RESCUING PASSENGERS FROM A DAMAGED TWIN OTTER IN THE ARCTIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, further to my question on November 26 at page 1,420 of Hansard, and further to the question of November 29 at page 1,456 of Hansard by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski), may I say that transportation in the Arctic and northern parts of the provinces is mainly by wheel, float and ski-equipped aircraft. In other words, if you travel, you must travel by air. The majority of carriers operating in the north are capable and competent, but flying in the north, where there is a lack of proper weather information, is extremely hazardous. I would like to use as an example aircraft movements out of the Thompson airport over the last nine months. There was a low of 2,712 aircraft movements per month to a high of 5,844 aircraft movements. This was over a nine-month period.
On November 18 a Twin Otter aircraft crashed on a flight from Rankin Inlet to Repulse Bay. I must say that the ELT- or Emergency Location Transmitter-signal was picked up very quickly and that a para-rescue medical troop was dropped to assist. I compliment the rescue crew involved, but the concern I have is about the lack of rescue equipment in the Arctic and northern areas of the provinces. People who fly on northern routes pay premium rates and must pay the compulsory airport user tax. The people of the north ask for no more and deserve no less than a guarantee that the Department of National Defence will maintain adequate search and rescue capabilities in the north, and I would like to stress that the facilities which are now at Edmonton should remain intact.

I am not ready to accept the argument that arrangements could not have been made to rescue the survivors of the November 18 accident if rescue equipment available from northern carriers had been used. I would like to recommend that in future when search and rescues are involved, the member of parliament for the area concerned be kept up to date and receive a copy of the report. The parliamentary

secretary said he could have given me a report if I had asked for it.
It is no secret that I am very concerned about the north. If the parliamentary secretary or the minister had forwarded the report to me I would not have taken the time of the House on this very serious matter. I want to stress again the importance of aircraft being equipped with ELT, emergency location transmitters.
A report of the crash in a newspaper dated November 25 said that Calm Air, the company that owned the Twin Otter aircraft, had to go back to search and rescue and plead with them to go in to rescue the crew.
I want to stress again the importance of having search and rescue facilities in the north where people have no other means of transport than to fly. I think they deserve full protection, and this is not only for adults who fly. In many of the disasters where aircraft go down, women and children are on board.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- ALLEGATION OF INFLUENCE IN GRANTING MORTGAGE TO YORK PLACE OF HAMILTON
CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- ALLEGATION OF INFLUENCE IN GRANTING MORTGAGE TO YORK PLACE OF HAMILTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate arises as a result of questions raised in the House on two previous occasions. The matter was raised once by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), and it involves a question directed to the former minister of state for urban affairs about a mortgage transaction concerning a property owned by York Place of Hamilton Incorporated, Hamilton, Ontario. To the original question asked by the hon. member for St. John's East the minister replied in part, as reported at page 501 of Hansard for October 27, 1976:
If there are any irregularities, certainly I want to be the first to know about them, and I will check into this.
After my colleague had asked for a public inquiry, the minister said in part, as reported at page 501 of Hansard:
Certainly, I will look at the allegations made and make necessary inquiries. As I am sure my hon. friend realizes, we certainly look for any discrepancies or anything which is out of order .. .
Not having heard anything for three weeks, I raised the matter again with the present minister. I asked whether, in view of the former minister's comments, there was any further information available on any irregularities, and I asked the minister if he had any information to give the House. The minister implied, that I had asked a question concerning a matter which was before the courts and that I should direct my question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). That was a different matter; but I subsequently asked the Minister of labour if he could tell the House what influence was exerted by his office which led to the decision of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Hamilton to increase the mortgage to York Place of Hamilton Incorporated. It would have been simple if the minister had said that in that case no influence had been exerted by any member of the staff of his office, but
December 6, 1976

the minister did not follow that course. He made some testy remarks and wondered if I wanted to add to the insinuation which had been made. He said in part, as reported at page 1,129 of Hansard:
If the hon. member wishes to add to such insinuations I would be more than happy to have him stand outside; then perhaps I could add him as co-defendant.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), added this comment, "Let us see the guts now."
I have raised this question outside the House for a very good reason: there is nearly $8 million of taxpayers' money involved in this case. And, so far as we know at the moment, there is a lack of security and certainly a lack of revenue for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The minister has not suggested to the House the reasons for twice increasing the original mortgage. Initially, in 1972, the mortgage for this property was approved in the amount of $5.7 million. Subsequently, in September, 1973, the mortgage was increased by $475,000. Late in 1974 it was further increased by $1,054,500. According to the affidavit filed by Central Mortgage and Housing in the courts in Hamilton, Ontario, there is now registered and under foreclosure a mortgage for the face figure of $7,229,500. Although less than $6 million has been advanced on this mortgage, according to the affidavit, the interest accrued to July 1, 1976 is more than $1.5 million. What this indicates, from a simple calculation, is that no interest had been paid on advances made between June 28, 1972 and July 27, 1975.
There are $350,000 worth of taxes owing to Hamilton for 1974, 1975 and 1976, and the affidavit states it would cost $550,000 to complete this project. So it is easy to see that CMHC, using taxpayers' dollars, will have $8 million and more invested in this place, and interest is accruing now at a monthly rate of $45,700.
The government can try to divert attention from the real issue by saying that the opposition is being mean to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and making false accusa-
Adjournment Debate
tions. He does not deny those accusations so we cannot tell whether they are false or not. But the question remains, and the minister has not explained why the mortgage amounts were twice increased after the inital deal had been made between the developer and CMHC, nor has he explained whether there is any possibility that any influence was exerted on the officials of CMHC in Hamilton.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Robert Gauthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- ALLEGATION OF INFLUENCE IN GRANTING MORTGAGE TO YORK PLACE OF HAMILTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hamilton office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation approved a loan under section 15 of the National Housing Act to York Place of Hamilton Inc. in December 1971, in the amount of $5,700,000. This project consists of two tower structures, one of 25 storeys containing 240 units and the second of 20 storeys with 197 units.
During the construction of this project, the borrower encountered two work stoppages. The first of these was a nine-month strike by elevator installers, and the second stretched over a 12-month period during a threatened lien action by the heating and plumbing contractor.
Between December, 1971, and December, 1974, the loan was increased twice to reach a final total of $7.2 million. The increases were caused by higher construction costs arising from these work stoppages, from changes in plans, and from difficult soil conditions which required changes in the foundations. At no time was a decision of the Hamilton office of CMHC reversed.
Mortgage advances are made by CMHC on the basis of the value of work in place, and the amount estimated as necessary to complete a project. When construction resumed after the extended work stoppages, steps were taken to ensure that the mortgage advances were applied strictly to project-related accounts and commitments.
